records.title: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.pageTitle: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.keywords: look unto me doctrine and covenants 6 36
records.text: Answers / Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 is not an isolated slogan. In context, the Lord directs Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery away from fear and toward Himself. The same Christ-centered movement appears across scripture: Paul tells disciples to rejoice in the Lord and rejoice in Christ Jesus, while Nephi declares, “we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ.” Together these passages form a study pattern for focusChrist: attention, remembrance, discipleship, and joy centered in the Savior. The revelation in context Explore and study Harmony, Pennsylvania: a setting of revelation A quiet lane leads toward an interpretive early nineteenth-century farmhouse. The scene recalls rural Harmony, Pennsylvania, where Oliver Cowdery sought assurance and received the Lord's tender command to look to Christ in every thought. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 The Setting: Oliver Cowdery Comes to Harmony Oliver Cowdery arrived at Joseph and Emma Smith's home in Harmony, Pennsylvania, on April 5, 1829. He began writing as Joseph's scribe on April 7. Before their meeting, Oliver had boarded with Joseph's parents and prayed about what he learned of the plates. The Church's historical account describes a private experience of peace that he had not shared. Doctrine and Covenants 6 recalled that experience while addressing his participation in the work. Earlier in the revelation, the Lord reminds Oliver of an experience of peace: “Did I not speak peace to your mind concerning the matter?” ( D&C 6:23 ). That reminder gives verse 36 added depth. Looking to Christ includes remembering light already received rather than allowing present fear to erase it. Read Oliver Cowdery's Gift Study D&C 6, 8, and 9 Church video Christ Is Risen; Faith in Him Will Move Mountains Connect the invitation to look to Christ with faith that acts, grows, and keeps turning toward Him. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Study lesson Look Unto Me: D&C 6 Seminary Study Explore the lesson’s questions about doubts and fears, and read the Savior’s invitation in its scriptural setting. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Read the verses as a sequence Explore and study Turn attention toward Christ Christ meets the viewer with a calm, reassuring gaze. In the quiet light of the setting sun, His expression offers a simple invitation: look to Him, remember His words and keep walking with faith. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:32-37 Doctrine and Covenants 6:32-37 Read the complete passage first. The reflections below follow its movement from Christ's presence to faithful action and His promise of eternal life. Verse 32: Christ is in the midst Jesus recalls His promise to disciples gathered in His name and applies it to Joseph and Oliver. Their work begins with His presence. Before asking how strong their faith feels, notice who speaks and where He says He is. Verse 33: Fear not to do good The Lord joins courage to goodness through the image of sowing and reaping. Consider a good action fear has made difficult: offering help, telling the truth, or making amends. This is an invitation to act faithfully, not a timetable for a particular result. Verse 34: Build upon His rock The verse acknowledges opposition rather than promising its absence. Christ's rock is the foundation of the reassurance. Ask what supports your choices when approval, comfort, or circumstances change. Verse 35: Receive mercy and continue Christ's words of non-condemnation accompany a call to leave sin and perform the commanded work soberly. Mercy and responsibility belong together. A useful reflection is: what can I turn from, and what work can I return to with greater care? Verse 36: Look unto Me The invitation directs attention to a person, Jesus Christ. Read it with the verses on either side: His presence, goodness, mercy, and sacrifice give trust its substance. Looking to Him can shape what you choose even before every question is settled. Verse 37: Behold the wounds The final verse directs attention to the Savior's wounded side, hands, and feet, then invites faithfulness and obedience. The Church's student manual says it is not known whether verses 32 and 37 refer to a literal or figurative experience. We can study what His words teach without deciding whether a visitation occurred. Why do Christ's wounds follow the invitation to look? The Seminary lesson pairs these verses and invites students to consider His Atonement and Resurrection. Compare 3 Nephi 11:10-17 : the risen Lord identifies Himself and invites the people to feel His wounds, becoming witnesses for themselves. Then read Alma 7:11-13 . Alma teaches of Christ taking upon Himself suffering, infirmities, death, and sins, and knowing how to help His people. Together, these passages direct our attention to both His power to redeem and His knowledge of human suffering. The wounds invite trust in the Savior who suffered and lives. Reflect: When you pray about pain, guilt, or fear, how might remembering the living Redeemer change what you ask Him for? Give yourself room to seek forgiveness, strength, or companionship without demanding that grief disappear. Church video Wherefore Didst Thou Doubt? Watch the account of Peter and the Savior on the water. Read Matthew 14:22-33 and notice Peter’s appeal for help. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video and transcript The Love of God Elder Benjamin M. Z. Tai connects Peter's appeal for rescue with looking to Christ in every thought. Watch for his invitations to remember God's love, pray for someone in need, and act. Which invitation could shape your next ordinary day? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Bring the scripture into the day Explore and study Bring an honest question with you Beside the open scriptures, a woman pauses to write down a question she has not yet resolved. The wide ocean and quiet moment remind us that faith can keep growing even before every answer comes. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22-23 Looking to Christ When Life Is Uncertain You can begin with the question you are carrying. These reflections are focusChrist study applications, offered alongside the scriptures and Church teachings linked here. What does “in every thought” mean? In Seek Christ in Every Thought , Elder Ulisses Soares describes bringing our minds and desires into harmony with Christ and choosing what is good each day. He also acknowledges that unwelcome thoughts can arise despite sincere effort. His teaching concerns how we respond and what we cultivate. Consider ordinary moments: preparing for work, listening to someone, or deciding how to answer a difficult message. A personal application is to pause and ask, “What would honesty, patience, and love require here?” Returning your attention to Christ can become a repeated practice. How does looking address doubt and fear? Read Matthew 14:27-33 all the way through. Peter becomes afraid and begins to sink, but he also calls for help. Jesus immediately reaches for him. The account includes rescue as well as correction. As a study application, distinguish a question you need to investigate from a fear that is preventing a good action. You can seek evidence, ask for help, and keep turning toward Christ. Do not use this passage to measure another person's faith by how calm they appear. What if an answer has not come? Oliver's remembered peace concerned a particular question. Remembering it did not make every later question identical. The historical account continues through his desire to translate, his unsuccessful attempt, further counsel, and his return to serving as scribe. Try writing two short notes: what you have reason to trust, and what remains unresolved. Preserve earlier light without treating it as a prediction about a new outcome. Hebrews 12:1-3 places looking to Jesus within patient endurance. The next step may be continued study, a conversation, or a responsibility you can fulfill while waiting. What if I do not know what God wants? In Jesus Christ Is the Strength of Youth , Elder Dieter F. Uchtdorf explains that gospel principles guide decisions without providing a separate yes or no for every possible choice. Christ remains the guide, and the person still chooses. For a decision before you, identify the relevant teaching, gather needed information, consider who is affected, and pray. Distinguish what is clearly right from a preference about an uncertain outcome. Choose a responsible next step and remain willing to learn. The video below can deepen this reflection; Prayer and Personal Revelation continues the study. Alma 37:36-37 brings this attention into an ordinary day: actions, thoughts, affections, counsel with God, rest at night, and gratitude in the morning. Choose one of those moments as a reminder to turn toward Him. Questions, knowledge, and revelation Stand Forever Explore Elder Lawrence E. Corbridge’s devotional, its four primary questions, and a guided study of faith and revelation on the dedicated study page. Open the Stand Forever study → A practical way to study Guided Study: Look, Remember, Talk, Rejoice, Act 1. Look Read D&C 6:32-37 and mark every statement about Jesus Christ. Ask what the passage teaches about who He is and what He promises. 2. Remember Read D&C 6:22-23 . Record one experience of peace, truth, help, or spiritual clarity you do not want fear to erase. 3. Talk Read 2 Nephi 25:26 . Share one thing you are learning about Christ with someone willing to listen, or write it for yourself. Speak honestly about what you understand and what you are still seeking. Explore and study Talk about what you are learning A father and daughter share an unhurried conversation while washing dishes together. Faith becomes part of family life when we speak of Christ with warmth, listen to one another and learn side by side. Read 2 Nephi 25:26 4. Rejoice Read Philippians 4:4 and 2 Nephi 25:26 . Write one reason you rejoice in Christ Himself, not merely in a hoped-for outcome. 5. Act Choose one faithful action consistent with Christ's teachings. Continue praying and studying without forcing certainty that has not come. Journal prompts What thought most often pulls my attention away from Christ? What truth in D&C 6:32-37 answers it? What has Christ already done that gives me reason to rejoice? What good action am I postponing because of fear? What would one faithful next step look like today? 2027 Church theme connection Rejoice in Christ The Church's 2027 youth theme is “Rejoice in Christ.” Church leaders have connected the theme with Philippians 4:4 , and the same phrase is being used for the 2027 Salt Lake Temple Celebration. That creates a natural companion to D&C 6:36 : the Savior we are invited to look toward is also the Savior in whom disciples rejoice. Philippians 4:4 “Rejoice in the Lord alway.” Read the surrounding chapter and notice how rejoicing is linked with prayer, gratitude, peace, disciplined thought, and strength through Christ. Philippians 3:1-8 Paul says believers “rejoice in Christ Jesus” and place no confidence in the flesh. Compare that with D&C 6:36 : confidence shifts away from self and toward Christ. 2 Nephi 25:23-26 Nephi explains why he writes and teaches so openly of the Savior: “we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ.” 2 Nephi 11:4-8 Nephi explains that he includes Isaiah so readers can lift up their hearts and rejoice. Prophecy, covenant, gathering, and the Messiah all become reasons to rejoice in Christ. How does looking to Christ become rejoicing in Him? Philippians 4:4-13 develops the connection. Paul moves from rejoicing to prayer with thanksgiving, then to peace guarding hearts and minds through Christ. He names things worthy of attention and urges disciples to practice what they have learned. His testimony of strength follows his account of both abundance and hunger. Joy in Christ does not depend on calling every circumstance pleasant. In Philippians 3:7-14 , Paul places knowing Christ above his former advantages and continues pressing forward. In 2 Nephi 11:4-8 , Nephi delights in the Redeemer, God's covenants, grace, and plan of deliverance. These are reasons for rejoicing rooted in who Christ is and what God provides. records.title: Harmony, Pennsylvania: a setting of revelation
records.pageTitle: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.text: The revelation in context Explore and study Harmony, Pennsylvania: a setting of revelation A quiet lane leads toward an interpretive early nineteenth-century farmhouse. The scene recalls rural Harmony, Pennsylvania, where Oliver Cowdery sought assurance and received the Lord's tender command to look to Christ in every thought. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 The Setting: Oliver Cowdery Comes to Harmony Oliver Cowdery arrived at Joseph and Emma Smith's home in Harmony, Pennsylvania, on April 5, 1829. He began writing as Joseph's scribe on April 7. Before their meeting, Oliver had boarded with Joseph's parents and prayed about what he learned of the plates. The Church's historical account describes a private experience of peace that he had not shared. Doctrine and Covenants 6 recalled that experience while addressing his participation in the work. Earlier in the revelation, the Lord reminds Oliver of an experience of peace: “Did I not speak peace to your mind concerning the matter?” ( D&C 6:23 ). That reminder gives verse 36 added depth. Looking to Christ includes remembering light already received rather than allowing present fear to erase it. Read Oliver Cowdery's Gift Study D&C 6, 8, and 9 Church video Christ Is Risen; Faith in Him Will Move Mountains Connect the invitation to look to Christ with faith that acts, grows, and keeps turning toward Him. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Study lesson Look Unto Me: D&C 6 Seminary Study Explore the lesson’s questions about doubts and fears, and read the Savior’s invitation in its scriptural setting. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

records.title: Turn attention toward Christ
records.pageTitle: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.text: Read the verses as a sequence Explore and study Turn attention toward Christ Christ meets the viewer with a calm, reassuring gaze. In the quiet light of the setting sun, His expression offers a simple invitation: look to Him, remember His words and keep walking with faith. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:32-37 Doctrine and Covenants 6:32-37 Read the complete passage first. The reflections below follow its movement from Christ's presence to faithful action and His promise of eternal life. Verse 32: Christ is in the midst Jesus recalls His promise to disciples gathered in His name and applies it to Joseph and Oliver. Their work begins with His presence. Before asking how strong their faith feels, notice who speaks and where He says He is. Verse 33: Fear not to do good The Lord joins courage to goodness through the image of sowing and reaping. Consider a good action fear has made difficult: offering help, telling the truth, or making amends. This is an invitation to act faithfully, not a timetable for a particular result. Verse 34: Build upon His rock The verse acknowledges opposition rather than promising its absence. Christ's rock is the foundation of the reassurance. Ask what supports your choices when approval, comfort, or circumstances change. Verse 35: Receive mercy and continue Christ's words of non-condemnation accompany a call to leave sin and perform the commanded work soberly. Mercy and responsibility belong together. A useful reflection is: what can I turn from, and what work can I return to with greater care? Verse 36: Look unto Me The invitation directs attention to a person, Jesus Christ. Read it with the verses on either side: His presence, goodness, mercy, and sacrifice give trust its substance. Looking to Him can shape what you choose even before every question is settled. Verse 37: Behold the wounds The final verse directs attention to the Savior's wounded side, hands, and feet, then invites faithfulness and obedience. The Church's student manual says it is not known whether verses 32 and 37 refer to a literal or figurative experience. We can study what His words teach without deciding whether a visitation occurred. Why do Christ's wounds follow the invitation to look? The Seminary lesson pairs these verses and invites students to consider His Atonement and Resurrection. Compare 3 Nephi 11:10-17 : the risen Lord identifies Himself and invites the people to feel His wounds, becoming witnesses for themselves. Then read Alma 7:11-13 . Alma teaches of Christ taking upon Himself suffering, infirmities, death, and sins, and knowing how to help His people. Together, these passages direct our attention to both His power to redeem and His knowledge of human suffering. The wounds invite trust in the Savior who suffered and lives. Reflect: When you pray about pain, guilt, or fear, how might remembering the living Redeemer change what you ask Him for? Give yourself room to seek forgiveness, strength, or companionship without demanding that grief disappear. Church video Wherefore Didst Thou Doubt? Watch the account of Peter and the Savior on the water. Read Matthew 14:22-33 and notice Peter’s appeal for help. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video and transcript The Love of God Elder Benjamin M. Z. Tai connects Peter's appeal for rescue with looking to Christ in every thought. Watch for his invitations to remember God's love, pray for someone in need, and act. Which invitation could shape your next ordinary day? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

records.title: Bring an honest question with you
records.pageTitle: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.text: Bring the scripture into the day Explore and study Bring an honest question with you Beside the open scriptures, a woman pauses to write down a question she has not yet resolved. The wide ocean and quiet moment remind us that faith can keep growing even before every answer comes. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22-23 Looking to Christ When Life Is Uncertain You can begin with the question you are carrying. These reflections are focusChrist study applications, offered alongside the scriptures and Church teachings linked here. What does “in every thought” mean? In Seek Christ in Every Thought , Elder Ulisses Soares describes bringing our minds and desires into harmony with Christ and choosing what is good each day. He also acknowledges that unwelcome thoughts can arise despite sincere effort. His teaching concerns how we respond and what we cultivate. Consider ordinary moments: preparing for work, listening to someone, or deciding how to answer a difficult message. A personal application is to pause and ask, “What would honesty, patience, and love require here?” Returning your attention to Christ can become a repeated practice. How does looking address doubt and fear? Read Matthew 14:27-33 all the way through. Peter becomes afraid and begins to sink, but he also calls for help. Jesus immediately reaches for him. The account includes rescue as well as correction. As a study application, distinguish a question you need to investigate from a fear that is preventing a good action. You can seek evidence, ask for help, and keep turning toward Christ. Do not use this passage to measure another person's faith by how calm they appear. What if an answer has not come? Oliver's remembered peace concerned a particular question. Remembering it did not make every later question identical. The historical account continues through his desire to translate, his unsuccessful attempt, further counsel, and his return to serving as scribe. Try writing two short notes: what you have reason to trust, and what remains unresolved. Preserve earlier light without treating it as a prediction about a new outcome. Hebrews 12:1-3 places looking to Jesus within patient endurance. The next step may be continued study, a conversation, or a responsibility you can fulfill while waiting. What if I do not know what God wants? In Jesus Christ Is the Strength of Youth , Elder Dieter F. Uchtdorf explains that gospel principles guide decisions without providing a separate yes or no for every possible choice. Christ remains the guide, and the person still chooses. For a decision before you, identify the relevant teaching, gather needed information, consider who is affected, and pray. Distinguish what is clearly right from a preference about an uncertain outcome. Choose a responsible next step and remain willing to learn. The video below can deepen this reflection; Prayer and Personal Revelation continues the study. Alma 37:36-37 brings this attention into an ordinary day: actions, thoughts, affections, counsel with God, rest at night, and gratitude in the morning. Choose one of those moments as a reminder to turn toward Him.

Talk Read 2 Nephi 25:26 . Share one thing you are learning about Christ with someone willing to listen, or write it for yourself. What has Christ already done that gives me reason to rejoice? What good action am I postponing because of fear? What would one faithful next step look like today?

records.title: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Answers / Prayer and revelation Latter-day Saints believe Heavenly Father hears sincere prayer and can give personal guidance through the Holy Ghost. They also believe spiritual impressions should be sought humbly, tested carefully, and kept within the responsibilities God has actually given a person. Personal revelation is a religious belief and spiritual practice, not a substitute for professional, legal, medical, or emergency help when those are needed. Prayer Is Communication with Heavenly Father Latter-day Saint prayer is directed to God the Father in the name of Jesus Christ. Prayer can include gratitude, confession, worship, requests for help, questions, and quiet listening. The purpose is not to force a preferred answer from God but to turn toward Him with sincerity and willingness to follow Him. What Is Personal Revelation? Personal revelation means divine guidance given to an individual for that person’s life, needs, relationships, and responsibilities. Latter-day Saints believe the Holy Ghost can bring peace, warning, understanding, remembrance, conviction, or quiet impressions. Revelation may come gradually rather than as a dramatic event. Recognize and remember Light Received Over Time Explore and study Step away and pray Jesus withdraws into the wilderness to pray alone. In the stillness, He shows the closeness, trust and renewal found in communion with the Father. Luke 5:16 In Using the Supernal Gift of Prayer , Elder Richard G. Scott describes seeking answers through prayer, thought, work, and patient action. He explains that understanding may arrive in portions. He also describes peace as a confirming witness in his own experience. Read his account as a personal testimony while making room for the questions you are still working through. Conference video · 14:58 Using the Supernal Gift of Prayer The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22-23 alongside his teaching. The Lord reminds Oliver of peace connected with a particular question. As a personal reflection, write what you remember and what it helped you understand. Keep any unresolved question beside it. Remembering an experience does not require adding certainty about something it did not answer. Watch and reflect: What have I already received that deserves patient attention? How Can Someone Prepare to Receive Guidance? Official Church teaching emphasizes prayer, scripture study, repentance, obedience, worship, and patient effort. A person may study a question, make a thoughtful decision, ask God for confirmation or correction, and remain open to an answer that differs from the original preference. How Can Spiritual Impressions Be Discerned? Latter-day Saints are taught not to treat every feeling as revelation. Genuine guidance should be consistent with God’s revealed commandments and the teachings of Jesus Christ. It should not authorize a person to control someone else’s agency or claim revelation for responsibilities that belong to another. Time, scripture, wise counsel, repeated impressions, and the fruits produced by a decision can help with discernment. What If No Answer Comes? Explore and study Keep a question open together Two sisters walk together while one shares a question she has not resolved. They do not need to force an answer; patient companionship can help faith endure while understanding grows. Read Alma 32 Waiting for an answer can be lonely, especially when the question matters deeply. A quiet prayer or an uncertain feeling is not, by itself, a verdict on your faith. Latter-day Saint teaching makes room for guidance that comes gradually and for thoughtful decisions made without a detailed instruction. You can keep seeking, talk with someone you trust, and take time to gather what you need. Conference video · 12:41 A Framework for Personal Revelation The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Watch with a question: Elder Dale G. Renlund explains how personal revelation relates to scripture, commandments, and your own responsibility to choose. As you listen, identify what is yours to decide and what belongs to someone else. Use the discernment exercise below to consider a next step while remaining open to further guidance. A Simple Place to Start Read James 1:5-6 , which invites those seeking wisdom to ask God. Doctrine and Covenants 8:2-3 describes guidance through the Holy Ghost in the mind and heart. You might name one question in your own words, spend a little time with the passage, and write down what you still need to understand. This is an invitation to pray, not a test of whether you feel something immediately. When You Are Unsure Whether a Feeling Is Guidance You can take an impression seriously while still considering it carefully. What does scripture teach about the decision? What information is missing? Does the choice respect another person's freedom? An urgent feeling alone does not settle those questions. In A Framework for Personal Revelation , Dale G. Renlund discusses scripture, personal responsibility, God's commandments, and openness to further guidance. His explanation is especially helpful when someone claims to know God's will for another person's major life decisions. Counsel can help you think; it does not remove your responsibility to choose. If your concern is that answers seem slow, the Church's Recognize That Revelation Is a Process offers further study. You might return to one question over time, without treating each prayer as a deadline for certainty. Discernment in an Ordinary Decision Explore and study Study, ask and keep a careful record A man writes beside an open book, placing prayer, thoughtful effort and a responsible next step together. The Lord's counsel to Oliver Cowdery joins seeking God's help with patient study. Doctrine and Covenants 9:7-9 Consider this everyday example as a focusChrist application: you feel drawn to contact a friend who has been distant. Elder Dale G. Renlund's framework directs attention to scripture, your responsibilities, God's commandments, and openness to further guidance. You can choose to offer a kind message. Your friend remains free to respond, decline, or ask for space. An impression to care for someone does not give you authority to decide their life. Explore and study Seek counsel with an open heart Two women pause beside their bicycles for a thoughtful conversation. Wise counsel can broaden a decision while leaving prayer, agency and responsibility with the person who must choose. Read Doctrine and Covenants 9 Questions to consider before acting Is this kind? Is it mine to decide? What information or consent do I need? These questions are personal reflection aids. They do not certify an impression as revelation. You can act thoughtfully while remaining willing to learn and change. Three Passages for a More Thoughtful Prayer Life Prayer without performance Matthew 6:5-13 places Jesus's teaching on prayer beside cautions about public display and empty repetition. The prayer He teaches includes God's will, daily needs, forgiveness, and deliverance. Consider which part is closest to your concern. You may pray in ordinary words; a polished explanation is not a prerequisite for seeking God. Explore and study Prayer before the Father A man prays privately beside an open book, echoing Jesus's teaching in Matthew 6 that prayer is sincere communion with the Father rather than a public performance. Read Matthew 6 Study and responsibility Doctrine and Covenants 9:7-9 was addressed to Oliver Cowdery in connection with translation. It describes studying a matter and asking God. Keep that setting in view: the passage should not become a rule that every faithful person must experience the same physical sensation for every decision. Compare it with the broader discernment guidance linked above. Faith can begin before certainty Alma 32:21, 26-28 distinguishes faith from perfect knowledge and invites a willingness to begin. As a personal exercise, separate what you know, what you hope, and what you still need to learn. That can help you bring a more honest question to prayer without claiming certainty you do not have. What should I write down? Consider the question, information you have gathered, counsel you have received, and a possible next step within your responsibility. Revisit it as circumstances change. A journal can support reflection, but it does not turn every thought into revelation. Official Sources and Further Study Prayer: Gospel Study Guide Revelation: Gospel Study Guide Holy Ghost: Gospel Study Guide Ask a Question Faith During Trials Where would you like to go next? Look to Christ while a question remains open Continue with remembered peace, everyday decisions, and the invitation to look unto Christ in every thought. When prayer accompanies difficulty Consider faithful action and support without requiring a particular feeling. Pause with Be Still Read Psalm 46 in context and try an optional reflection about attention and agency. Watch and reflect on listening Explore three official videos on prayer, quiet attention and spiritual understanding, with scripture to read alongside them.

Conference video · 14:58 Using the Supernal Gift of Prayer The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22-23 alongside his teaching. The Lord reminds Oliver of peace connected with a particular question. As a personal reflection, write what you remember and what it helped you understand. Keep any unresolved question beside it. Remembering an experience does not require adding certainty about something it did not answer. Watch and reflect: What have I already received that deserves patient attention?

records.title: What If No Answer Comes?
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Explore and study Keep a question open together Two sisters walk together while one shares a question she has not resolved. They do not need to force an answer; patient companionship can help faith endure while understanding grows. Read Alma 32 Waiting for an answer can be lonely, especially when the question matters deeply. A quiet prayer or an uncertain feeling is not, by itself, a verdict on your faith. Latter-day Saint teaching makes room for guidance that comes gradually and for thoughtful decisions made without a detailed instruction. You can keep seeking, talk with someone you trust, and take time to gather what you need. Conference video · 12:41 A Framework for Personal Revelation The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Watch with a question: Elder Dale G. Renlund explains how personal revelation relates to scripture, commandments, and your own responsibility to choose. As you listen, identify what is yours to decide and what belongs to someone else. Use the discernment exercise below to consider a next step while remaining open to further guidance.

records.title: Discernment in an Ordinary Decision
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Explore and study Study, ask and keep a careful record A man writes beside an open book, placing prayer, thoughtful effort and a responsible next step together. The Lord's counsel to Oliver Cowdery joins seeking God's help with patient study. Doctrine and Covenants 9:7-9 Consider this everyday example as a focusChrist application: you feel drawn to contact a friend who has been distant. Elder Dale G. Renlund's framework directs attention to scripture, your responsibilities, God's commandments, and openness to further guidance. You can choose to offer a kind message. Your friend remains free to respond, decline, or ask for space. An impression to care for someone does not give you authority to decide their life. Explore and study Seek counsel with an open heart Two women pause beside their bicycles for a thoughtful conversation. Wise counsel can broaden a decision while leaving prayer, agency and responsibility with the person who must choose. Read Doctrine and Covenants 9 Questions to consider before acting Is this kind? Is it mine to decide? What information or consent do I need? These questions are personal reflection aids. They do not certify an impression as revelation. You can act thoughtfully while remaining willing to learn and change.

records.title: Three Passages for a More Thoughtful Prayer Life
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Prayer without performance Matthew 6:5-13 places Jesus's teaching on prayer beside cautions about public display and empty repetition. The prayer He teaches includes God's will, daily needs, forgiveness, and deliverance. Consider which part is closest to your concern. You may pray in ordinary words; a polished explanation is not a prerequisite for seeking God. Explore and study Prayer before the Father A man prays privately beside an open book, echoing Jesus's teaching in Matthew 6 that prayer is sincere communion with the Father rather than a public performance. Read Matthew 6 Study and responsibility Doctrine and Covenants 9:7-9 was addressed to Oliver Cowdery in connection with translation. It describes studying a matter and asking God. Keep that setting in view: the passage should not become a rule that every faithful person must experience the same physical sensation for every decision. Compare it with the broader discernment guidance linked above. Faith can begin before certainty Alma 32:21, 26-28 distinguishes faith from perfect knowledge and invites a willingness to begin. As a personal exercise, separate what you know, what you hope, and what you still need to learn. That can help you bring a more honest question to prayer without claiming certainty you do not have. What should I write down? Consider the question, information you have gathered, counsel you have received, and a possible next step within your responsibility. Revisit it as circumstances change. A journal can support reflection, but it does not turn every thought into revelation.

records.title: Is this the restored Church of Jesus Christ?
records.pageTitle: Is this the restored Church of Jesus Christ?
records.text: Answers / Stand Forever / The restored Church What does it mean to speak of the restored Church of Jesus Christ? Study its teachings about the Savior, authority, covenants, and service through primary sources, then connect those claims with thoughtful personal inquiry. Study the claim and the life it invites This is the fourth foundational question in the Stand Forever study. Latter-day Saints believe that Jesus Christ restored His Church through Joseph Smith, including priesthood authority and ordinances. Understanding that belief involves more than learning an organization’s name: it includes asking what the Church teaches about Christ and what its members covenant to do. Use two pages in your notebook. On one, record a claim and the source that makes it. On the other, record your questions and observations. A historical question, a doctrinal question, and a personal spiritual question may call for different kinds of inquiry. Keeping them distinct lets you examine each carefully without losing the relationship between them. Begin with one scripture section. The videos and linked companion studies give you places to continue, so this page can support several study sessions rather than a single quick visit. 1. Begin with Jesus Christ as the foundation Ephesians 2 describes reconciliation through Christ and a community whose members are no longer strangers. Verses 19–22 use the image of a household and a building, with apostles and prophets in the foundation and Jesus Christ as the chief cornerstone. The chapter places belonging within the redeeming work of Christ. Explore and study Keep Jesus Christ at the center Jesus Christ stands among attentive disciples as their teacher and sure foundation. Around Him, strangers can become fellow citizens in a covenant community built upon His peace. Read Ephesians 2:13–22 Read verses 13–22 together. Ask how the architectural image serves the chapter’s larger account of reconciliation. Latter-day Saints connect this language with their belief in a Church led through apostles and prophets. The passage itself does not narrate nineteenth-century events; studying that connection also requires the Restoration sources below. Read Ephesians 2:13–22 Keep Christ central What does this passage say brings people near? How should a community centered on Jesus Christ treat a person who feels like a stranger? Study the identity and redeeming work of Jesus Christ → 2. Read an early account of belief and order Doctrine and Covenants 20 combines an account of the Church’s beginnings with teachings, responsibilities, and ordinances. Its opening identifies the Church’s organization in 1830. Later passages describe faith in Jesus Christ, repentance, baptism, and the Holy Ghost, as well as responsibilities within the community. Explore and study Christ at the heart of the restored Church An open book, paper and inkwell bring the written revelation behind the Church's 1830 organization into view. Its doctrine, ordinances and community life all lead back to Jesus Christ. Read Doctrine and Covenants 20 For an initial reading, pair verses 1–12 with verses 17–37. Mark the difference between the historical statements and the theological claims. This is a primary religious text for what Latter-day Saints understand the restored Church to teach. Reading it carefully helps you ask more specific questions about authority, scripture, and the meaning of membership. Read Doctrine and Covenants 20 Make a source-based question Which claim would I like to understand more fully? What original account or passage would help me investigate it? Continue with Joseph Smith and the historical record → For a contemporary statement of these beliefs, watch the message below and read the Restoration proclamation within its transcript. Video · Reflection image Hear Him Russell M. Nelson teaches about hearing Jesus Christ and presents the 2020 Restoration proclamation. Read the proclamation within the full message. Official Church video · April 2020. Reflection image: Jesus Christ studying with two attentive listeners. Read the full message 3. See the responsibilities of belonging Explore and study Consider a covenant in practice A family arrives at an older neighbor's door with groceries and a warm meal. In that simple offering, the baptismal promise to bear burdens and give comfort becomes personal. Mosiah 18:8-10 In Mosiah 18 , Alma teaches people preparing for baptism. Verses 8–10 describe willingness to bear burdens, mourn with others, offer comfort, and stand as witnesses of God. These commitments give concrete meaning to a covenant community. Read through verse 16 to keep the invitation connected to the account of baptism. The passage helps you examine what discipleship asks of people in relation to one another. As an application, consider a place where you have received care and a person whose burden you could help carry. Service is worth practicing thoughtfully, without assuming you already know another person’s needs. Read Mosiah 18:8–16 Turn a covenant into care Who needs companionship, practical help, or patient listening? What small act could I offer respectfully this week? 4. Examine the gospel at the center In 3 Nephi 27 , the disciples ask Jesus about the name of the Church. His answer connects His name with His gospel. Verses 13–22 focus on His mission, His being lifted upon the cross, repentance, baptism, and sanctification through receiving the Holy Ghost. Explore and study Examine the gospel Christ describes Jesus Christ teaches a disciple who listens closely. His gospel is more than a statement of belief; it is a call to repent, follow Him and become changed through His grace. Read 3 Nephi 27 Read the chapter’s opening alongside that explanation. The name and the life of the community belong together in this account. When exploring the restored Church, look at what its sources teach about Jesus Christ, how ordinances point toward Him, and what discipleship asks people to become. Observations about a community can be meaningful while still leaving historical or doctrinal questions to investigate directly. Read 3 Nephi 27:1–22 Notice the connection How does Jesus describe His gospel here? Which part would you like to study or practice more intentionally? Explore temples and covenant worship → Watch with a question in mind Continue from the Restoration message above into the invitation to belong and serve. Keep the original transcript beside your notes. Identify a teaching, follow its scripture references, and separate the speaker’s words from your own application. Video · Original publisher thumbnail Come, Join with Us Dieter F. Uchtdorf speaks about belonging, discipleship, and making room for people with questions. Consider how an invitation becomes daily community life. Official Church YouTube channel · October 2013 Read the full message Connect careful study with lived discipleship Read: choose one original passage and summarize its claim in a sentence. Compare: follow a related reference or companion study instead of relying on a quotation alone. Reflect: record what is clearer and what remains a real question. Act: choose an appropriate step in prayer, service, conversation, or further research. If you study with others, give each person room to say what they understand without requiring a declaration of certainty. You can ask a Church member how a covenant shapes daily life, read a historical account together, or offer help in your own community. An encounter is one part of inquiry; it does not replace reading the sources. Explore and study Study a claim together Three friends gather around a source, listening carefully and giving each person room for a sincere question about belief or discipleship. Read Mosiah 18 Return to your notes after your chosen step. Which question became more specific? What source should come next? A coherent study grows through these connections, not through the number of tabs you open. Bring a source-based question to Ask , or explore General Conference for more messages. Check AI-assisted explanations against their original references. Read the original sources The scripture explanations above draw on Ephesians 2 , Doctrine and Covenants 20 , Mosiah 18 , and 3 Nephi 27 . The two videos link to official Church publications. Reading sequences and reflection prompts are focusChrist study aids, not additional Church doctrine. Ephesians 2: Reconciliation and the cornerstone Doctrine and Covenants 20: Organization, belief, and ordinances Mosiah 18: A covenant community 3 Nephi 27: The name of the Church and Christ’s gospel Continue the four-question study These studies belong together. Keep your notes as you move between them: what the sources teach, what you have experienced, what remains open, and what you want to do next. records.title: Stand Forever
records.text: Answers / Stand Forever Study foundational questions, honest inquiry, and revelation through Elder Lawrence E. Corbridge’s January 22, 2019 BYU devotional. Read the complete source beside this focusChrist study guide. Watch and study · Scripture Central Stand Forever video series ▶ Watch the trailer With Elder Lawrence E. Corbridge Explore Scripture Central’s series on enduring discipleship in Jesus Christ. The series expands on the message of Elder Corbridge’s 2019 BYU devotional, which you can study below. Begin with episode 1, “Will You Stand, or Will You Go Away?” Or open the publisher’s full playlist to choose from its available videos. Open full playlist Start with Episode 1 Published by Scripture Central . The playlist on YouTube contains the publisher’s current selection. About the series and speaker . Questions, knowledge, and revelation Stand Forever In his January 22, 2019 BYU devotional, Elder Lawrence E. Corbridge asks how disciples can remain grounded when they encounter difficult claims, uncertainty, or an overwhelming number of questions. His answer is not to stop asking. It is to understand which questions are foundational, use every honest way of learning available, and seek a confirming witness through the Holy Ghost. Keep the Savior in the center of the inquiry. A secondary question deserves careful study, but it should not be asked to carry the entire weight of faith in God, Jesus Christ, the Restoration, or the Church. The four primary questions The address identifies four foundational questions. These are presented as the questions that give spiritual orientation to the many historical, doctrinal, cultural, and personal questions a disciple may continue to examine. Explore and study Stay with one honest question A woman sits with an open book and notebook, giving one important question her full attention. Her quiet study joins honest thought with a heart willing to seek God in prayer. Read Doctrine and Covenants 9:7–9 Choose a question to open its complete study. Read a passage in context, explore its video resources, then use the connected studies to continue at your own pace. God Is there a God who is our Father? Consider what scripture, experience, creation, prayer, and revelation contribute to this question. Open study Jesus Christ Is Jesus Christ the Son of God and Savior of the world? Let His identity, teachings, Atonement, and Resurrection remain central. Open study Joseph Smith Was Joseph Smith a prophet? Study the historical record, revealed scripture, prophetic claims, fruits, and your own spiritual inquiry. Open study The restored Church Is The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints God’s kingdom on the earth? Examine its authority claims, covenants, doctrine, mission, and fruits. Open study Primary does not mean “only.” Elder Corbridge explicitly teaches that questions are important. The distinction invites proportion and order, not avoidance. Difficult secondary questions can still be researched honestly, patiently, and from reliable sources. Four ways of learning The talk describes four methods that begin with a question. Together they invite action, careful reasoning, disciplined study, and revelation rather than dependence on a single kind of evidence. Explore and study Follow the truth with patience A student studies an original source beside her own notes. She follows what the record can establish and has the humility to leave unanswered what it cannot. Read Doctrine and Covenants 93:24 Experience and action Scientific Form a question, act or experiment where appropriate, observe the result, and revise what you think. Gospel truth can be tested through faithful practice and its fruits. Evidence and reason Analytical Gather relevant evidence, organize it, weigh it fairly, notice assumptions, and draw conclusions that remain proportionate to what the evidence supports. The written word Academic Read deeply and in context. Compare scripture, original records, responsible scholarship, and authoritative teaching rather than relying on isolated summaries. The things of God Divine Seek knowledge through the Holy Ghost. Prayer and revelation do not remove the need to act, reason, or study; they address spiritual truth through the Spirit of God. A faithful inquiry practice Use this sequence with a question you genuinely carry. It creates room for evidence and uncertainty while keeping your relationship with Jesus Christ visible. Explore and study Give a record its context Shelved records and a prepared reading table emphasize the care required to preserve evidence and study it in context. Read Doctrine and Covenants 9:7–9 Name the question precisely. Replace a broad fear with the specific claim, event, passage, or doctrine you need to understand. Classify without dismissing. Is it one of the four primary questions, or a secondary question connected to one of them? Gather the strongest sources. Read the primary record and its context. Distinguish the source itself from another person’s interpretation. Use all four methods. Note experience, evidence, written study, and spiritual impressions without pretending they are identical kinds of knowledge. Record what is known and unknown. Write what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain, and what additional source would help. Return to Christ. Ask what the inquiry teaches about the Savior and what faithful action is appropriate while study continues. Read the talk beside Doctrine and Covenants 6 Elder Corbridge closes with Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 . The surrounding revelation to Oliver Cowdery adds a compassionate pattern for seeking and standing. Remember peace received Verses 22–23 invite Oliver to remember the peace that came when he sought a witness. Spiritual memory can be evidence without ending every later question. Do good without fear Verses 33–34 join faithful action with reassurance. A seeker can continue doing good while understanding develops. Look unto Christ Verses 36–37 direct every thought toward Christ and answer fear with His presence, sacrifice, and promise of a place with Him. Scriptures for deeper study These passages are used in the address or closely support its pattern of asking, studying, receiving light, and standing on revelation. Open one passage at a time and record what it contributes to the question you are studying. D&C 9:7–9 Study it out, ask, and recognize spiritual confirmation. D&C 50:23–24 Distinguish what edifies and continue receiving light. D&C 93:24 Consider truth as knowledge of things as they are, were, and will be. Alma 32:27–28 Experiment upon the word and observe what begins to grow. Moroni 10:4–5 Study, remember, ponder, and ask God with sincere intent. Matthew 16:15–18 Peter’s witness of Christ illustrates the rock of revelation. Companion messages Continue the study with three apostolic messages that make room for honest questions while inviting deliberate faith and forward movement in Jesus Christ. General conference “Lord, I Believe” Elder Jeffrey R. Holland invites disciples to acknowledge questions honestly while beginning with the faith they already have. General conference Faith Is Not by Chance, but by Choice Elder Neil L. Andersen teaches that honest questions matter and that faith grows through deliberate choices, sincere study, and seeking answers from God. General conference The Power of Spiritual Momentum President Russell M. Nelson offers five actions for building spiritual momentum and moving forward through uncertainty and opposition. Seven-day “Stand Forever” study Read the full address once without stopping to resolve every reference. Write the four primary questions in your own words. Choose one secondary question and define it precisely. Identify one source or action for each method of learning. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22–23 and record a remembered experience of peace. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:32–37 and mark every invitation or promise from Christ. Write what you know, what you are still studying, and one faithful next step. Reflection and journal prompts Which primary question most shapes the way I understand the others? Am I asking a secondary question to decide more than its evidence can establish? Which method of learning have I used well, and which have I neglected? What do I know from experience, evidence, study, or the Holy Ghost? What can remain honestly unresolved while I continue looking to Christ? Read or Watch Stand Forever Study D&C 6:22–23, 32–37 Carry a question with care Explore and study Carry the question prayerfully A woman pauses in prayer beside an open book, bringing both faith and an honest question before God. Moroni's invitation centers that search on sincerity, real intent and faith in Christ. Read Moroni 10:4–5 Optional focusChrist reflection Which question needs clearer wording? What do I know from a source, what am I inferring, and what still needs patient study? Official sources and original address This guide draws from the BYU address and the scripture passages linked above. The inquiry practice is a focusChrist study aid. Lawrence E. Corbridge, Stand Forever: January 22, 2019 Doctrine and Covenants 6 Continue your study Explore and study Choose a faithful next step A man holds an umbrella over an older neighbor as rain falls around them. It is a small kindness, freely given, and a gentle answer to the Lord's invitation to do good without fear. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:33–34 Look Unto Me Prayer and revelation Bring a study question

Open study Primary does not mean “only.” Elder Corbridge explicitly teaches that questions are important. The distinction invites proportion and order, not avoidance. Difficult secondary questions can still be researched honestly, patiently, and from reliable sources. Four ways of learning The talk describes four methods that begin with a question. Together they invite action, careful reasoning, disciplined study, and revelation rather than dependence on a single kind of evidence. Explore and study Follow the truth with patience A student studies an original source beside her own notes. She follows what the record can establish and has the humility to leave unanswered what it cannot. Read Doctrine and Covenants 93:24 Experience and action Scientific Form a question, act or experiment where appropriate, observe the result, and revise what you think. Gospel truth can be tested through faithful practice and its fruits. Evidence and reason Analytical Gather relevant evidence, organize it, weigh it fairly, notice assumptions, and draw conclusions that remain proportionate to what the evidence supports. The written word Academic Read deeply and in context. Compare scripture, original records, responsible scholarship, and authoritative teaching rather than relying on isolated summaries. The things of God Divine Seek knowledge through the Holy Ghost. Prayer and revelation do not remove the need to act, reason, or study; they address spiritual truth through the Spirit of God. A faithful inquiry practice Use this sequence with a question you genuinely carry. It creates room for evidence and uncertainty while keeping your relationship with Jesus Christ visible. Explore and study Give a record its context Shelved records and a prepared reading table emphasize the care required to preserve evidence and study it in context. Read Doctrine and Covenants 9:7–9 Name the question precisely. Replace a broad fear with the specific claim, event, passage, or doctrine you need to understand. Classify without dismissing. Is it one of the four primary questions, or a secondary question connected to one of them? Gather the strongest sources. Read the primary record and its context. Distinguish the source itself from another person’s interpretation. Use all four methods. Note experience, evidence, written study, and spiritual impressions without pretending they are identical kinds of knowledge. Record what is known and unknown. Write what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain, and what additional source would help. Return to Christ. Ask what the inquiry teaches about the Savior and what faithful action is appropriate while study continues. Read the talk beside Doctrine and Covenants 6 Elder Corbridge closes with Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 . The surrounding revelation to Oliver Cowdery adds a compassionate pattern for seeking and standing. Remember peace received Verses 22–23 invite Oliver to remember the peace that came when he sought a witness. Spiritual memory can be evidence without ending every later question. Do good without fear Verses 33–34 join faithful action with reassurance. A seeker can continue doing good while understanding develops. Look unto Christ Verses 36–37 direct every thought toward Christ and answer fear with His presence, sacrifice, and promise of a place with Him. Scriptures for deeper study These passages are used in the address or closely support its pattern of asking, studying, receiving light, and standing on revelation. Open one passage at a time and record what it contributes to the question you are studying. D&C 9:7–9 Study it out, ask, and recognize spiritual confirmation. D&C 50:23–24 Distinguish what edifies and continue receiving light. D&C 93:24 Consider truth as knowledge of things as they are, were, and will be. Alma 32:27–28 Experiment upon the word and observe what begins to grow. Moroni 10:4–5 Study, remember, ponder, and ask God with sincere intent. Matthew 16:15–18 Peter’s witness of Christ illustrates the rock of revelation. Companion messages Continue the study with three apostolic messages that make room for honest questions while inviting deliberate faith and forward movement in Jesus Christ. General conference “Lord, I Believe” Elder Jeffrey R. Holland invites disciples to acknowledge questions honestly while beginning with the faith they already have. General conference Faith Is Not by Chance, but by Choice Elder Neil L. Andersen teaches that honest questions matter and that faith grows through deliberate choices, sincere study, and seeking answers from God. General conference The Power of Spiritual Momentum President Russell M. Nelson offers five actions for building spiritual momentum and moving forward through uncertainty and opposition. Seven-day “Stand Forever” study Read the full address once without stopping to resolve every reference. Write the four primary questions in your own words. Choose one secondary question and define it precisely. Identify one source or action for each method of learning. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22–23 and record a remembered experience of peace. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:32–37 and mark every invitation or promise from Christ. Write what you know, what you are still studying, and one faithful next step. Reflection and journal prompts Which primary question most shapes the way I understand the others? Am I asking a secondary question to decide more than its evidence can establish? Which method of learning have I used well, and which have I neglected? What do I know from experience, evidence, study, or the Holy Ghost? What can remain honestly unresolved while I continue looking to Christ? Read or Watch Stand Forever Study D&C 6:22–23, 32–37
