records.title: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Answers / Life after death Latter-day Saints believe death is a temporary separation of body and spirit, not the end of personal existence. Because Jesus Christ rose from the dead, every person will eventually be resurrected. Begin with Jesus Christ and the people He comforted. Then follow the scriptures through the spirit world, resurrection, and judgment. Each picture opens a study panel with its own scripture reading and a full-size view. You can follow the reading journey in order or begin with the question closest to your heart. This page explains the Latter-day Saint plan-of-salvation framework. It is not an official Church publication; official sources are linked throughout the study. A Savior who knows sorrow Christ Meets Us in Grief Martha came to Jesus after her brother Lazarus had died. In John 11:21-27 , she speaks of her loss and her belief in a future resurrection. Jesus directs that hope to Himself. The promise of life rests in who He is and what He can do. Explore and study Christ listens to Martha Martha brings her loss and her belief to Jesus. His promise of resurrection begins with an invitation to trust Him. John 11:21–27 Later, when Mary and those with her are weeping, Jesus weeps too. Read John 11:32-36 beside His conversation with Martha. Confidence in resurrection and compassion for present sorrow belong in the same account. Tears do not disprove faith. The raising of Lazarus in John 11:38-44 witnesses Christ's power over death. Lazarus returned to mortal life; the Savior's Resurrection opens the way to immortal life. That distinction helps us read the miracle with hope while recognizing that loved ones are not ordinarily restored to us during mortality. Pause and reflect: a promise and a sorrow Notice what Martha believes and what still hurts. If you wish, name one promise you want to hold and one loss you need to speak about. Prayer can include both. If you are accompanying someone who mourns, begin by listening to what they want to share. The foundation of Christian hope Mary Magdalene Sees the Living Lord Explore and study Morning at the empty tomb Morning light enters an open garden tomb, holding the astonishment and hope of the Resurrection. Mary's grief gives way when the risen Jesus calls her by name. John 20:1-18 The empty tomb is only the beginning of Mary's morning. In John 20:11-18 , she is still weeping and thinks Jesus' body has been taken. When He calls her by name, she recognizes Him. She then tells the disciples that she has seen the Lord. John presents a personal encounter with the risen Jesus. Explore and study Mary recognizes the risen Savior Jesus calls Mary by name, and she recognizes Him. Her encounter turns the morning of sorrow toward the news that He lives. John 20:11–18 A witness that reaches into personal loss In And There Shall Be No More Death , Elder Paul V. Johnson reflects on resurrection after his adult daughter's death from cancer. He teaches that Christ makes the reunion of spirit and body permanent. Read his message beside Mary's witness: Christian hope rests in a living Savior. The message includes illness and bereavement. You may prefer to read a little at a time, beginning with the teaching about resurrection. General conference video and text And There Shall Be No More Death The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2016 Pause and reflect: what changes when Christ is risen? Compare Mary's concern at the tomb with the message she carries to the disciples. What does Christ's Resurrection let you hope for? Write your own question beside the passage and return to it as the study continues. The spirit continues to live What Happens Between Death and Resurrection? At death, body and spirit separate. Alma 40:11-14 describes spirits continuing to live while they await resurrection. Alma speaks of paradise as peace and rest for the righteous, and of a painful condition for the wicked. These are conditions in the spirit world, distinct from the final reunion of body and spirit. Explore and study Hope between death and resurrection In a quiet garden, an older man pauses over Alma's words about the life of the spirit after death. The promise of resurrection through Jesus Christ brings hope close to the memories he carries. Read Alma 40 Read on to Alma 40:21-23 . The body and spirit are to be reunited, and a person is brought before God. Keeping these teachings together helps us avoid treating the spirit world as the end of the story. The Church study guide on the spirit world offers further passages and questions for careful study. Christ's work reaches those who have died Doctrine and Covenants 138:12-19 describes faithful spirits awaiting the Savior's arrival and the redemption He makes possible. The vision then explains how His message reaches others: in Doctrine and Covenants 138:29-35 , Christ commissions messengers from among the righteous to teach those in darkness. They teach faith, repentance, and the ordinances of the gospel. The vision does not describe salvation as automatic. Doctrine and Covenants 138:58-59 connects redemption with repentance and the ordinances of God's house. Latter-day Saints perform proxy ordinances in temples because those who have died cannot perform these earthly ordinances for themselves. Each person remains free to accept or reject what is offered. Continue with the temple study to explore that connection. General conference video and text The Redemption of the Dead and the Testimony of Jesus The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2000 Elder Christofferson explains how temple service bears witness of Christ’s Resurrection and the reach of His Atonement. He makes clear that people who have died retain their agency: proxy ordinances take effect only if they accept them. General conference video and text The Vision of the Redemption of the Dead The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2018 President Ballard recalls the losses Joseph F. Smith endured and invites us to study the revelation he received. Doctrine and Covenants 138:29-35 describes Christ commissioning messengers to carry His gospel to the dead. Pause and reflect: hope with humility Find what the vision says Christ and His messengers do. Then separate those teachings from questions it does not answer about a loved one's daily experience. We can trust God's care without claiming to know where a particular person is or what they are doing. Christ's victory over physical death Everyone Will Be Resurrected When the risen Jesus comes among His disciples in Luke 24:36-43 , He offers peace and invites them to see His hands and feet. He distinguishes His resurrected body from a spirit and eats in their presence. Resurrection is more than the continued life of the spirit after death. Explore and study Peace among the disciples Christ comes among His disciples and offers peace. His hands and His presence testify that the One they mourned is alive. John 20:19–23 Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 that Christ's Resurrection makes resurrection possible for all. Later, in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 and 1 Corinthians 15:51-57 , he describes mortality giving way to immortality and gives thanks to God for victory through Jesus Christ. This universal gift is not something we earn by being strong enough or by grieving in a particular way. Thomas and the witness we receive Explore and study An invitation to Thomas The Savior invites Thomas to witness for himself. John records Thomas’s answer of faith and Christ’s blessing on those who believe without seeing. John 20:24–29 Thomas was absent when Jesus first appeared to the assembled disciples. In John 20:24-29 , Jesus later invites Thomas to behold His hands and believe. The account also speaks to readers who have not seen Him. John explains his purpose in John 20:30-31 : his written witness invites belief in Jesus Christ and life through His name. Questions about resurrection can be brought to these witnesses patiently. Consider what they testify that Jesus did, then what His living reality means for the person you miss. Hope does not require you to invent details that scripture has not supplied. Another witness of the risen Savior Jesus Christ Ministers in the Book of Mormon The Book of Mormon adds its witness of the same risen Jesus. 3 Nephi 11:1-12 places a multitude near the temple in Bountiful, where the Father introduces His Son and Jesus declares His identity and saving mission. The people encounter the Savior who has overcome death. His ministry among them shows the compassion of the One in whom their eternal hope rests. One by one, they come to Him Explore and study One by one One person steps forward while others wait. The account gives each witness a place in the multitude’s testimony that Jesus Christ has risen. 3 Nephi 11:14–17 In 3 Nephi 11:14-17 , Jesus invites the people to feel the marks in His hands, feet, and side. They approach individually and become witnesses of His living reality. Read this beside the New Testament witnesses: the Resurrection is the foundation of their worship and hope. Notice the time given to each person in a large multitude. As a reflection, consider the difference between knowing that Christ loves humanity and trusting that you matter to Him personally. He teaches a life shaped by mercy Explore and study Blessed are the merciful The risen Savior teaches mercy, purity of heart, and peacemaking. His victory over death also calls His followers into a life shaped by His love. 3 Nephi 12:3–9 The risen Lord's teaching includes comfort for those who mourn and blessings for the merciful, pure in heart, and peacemakers. Read 3 Nephi 12:3-9 slowly. His invitation joins hope for God's kingdom with the kind of people we are becoming now. Choose one of these teachings to carry into an ordinary relationship. A merciful response, a patient conversation, or a sincere effort toward peace can be part of discipleship while we look forward to life with God. He receives the sick and afflicted Explore and study He healed them every one Christ invites the people to bring those who are afflicted. The scripture records His compassion and the healing of every person brought to Him. 3 Nephi 17:5–10 3 Nephi 17:7-10 records the people bringing those who are sick or afflicted to Jesus, and His healing them. His compassion reaches those who suffer and the people who help them come. The account witnesses His power and mercy; it does not give a timetable for every healing we seek today. He kneels and prays for them Explore and study He prayed for them Jesus kneels and prays to the Father. The witnesses describe their joy, while leaving the full words of His prayer unrecorded. 3 Nephi 17:12–20 In 3 Nephi 17:15-20 , Jesus kneels upon the earth and prays to the Father. The witnesses describe joy beyond their ability to express. The prayer's full words are not recorded, so we let their witness stand without supplying a speech for Him. He blesses the children individually Explore and study A blessing for each child The children receive His attention one by one. Read the whole passage to follow the blessing and the angels’ ministry that comes afterward. 3 Nephi 17:21–24 3 Nephi 17:21-24 describes Jesus weeping, blessing little children one by one, and praying for them. The people then see angels minister to the children. This tender scene gives us another view of the risen Lord's love. It describes His ministry to living children, rather than a detailed picture of a child's experience after death. If you are mourning a child, you can linger with the Savior's care here and continue to the study on child loss for the specific promises about little children. He gives bread and fills their souls Explore and study He gives bread and fills their souls Christ gives bread to His disciples and directs them to share it. The people stand, receive the bread and wine, and are filled with the Spirit. 3 Nephi 20:1–9 In 3 Nephi 20:1-9 , Jesus directs the people to stand, breaks and blesses bread, and gives it to His disciples to share. He also gives wine and teaches the meaning of partaking. The people receive the Spirit and glorify Him. Remembering the living Savior draws their worship toward the One who gives lasting life. He asks that the resurrection witness be recorded Explore and study Preserving the resurrection witness Christ asks about the missing account of saints who rose and ministered. Nephi remembers, and the record is completed so this witness can be preserved. 3 Nephi 23:6–14 When Nephi brings the record in 3 Nephi 23:6-14 , Jesus asks about the fulfillment of Samuel's prophecy that saints would rise and minister to many. The disciples confirm that it happened, and the missing account is written. This moment connects careful recordkeeping with testimony of Christ's victory over death. The witness matters enough to preserve for those who will read later. He listens to the disciples' desires Explore and study The desire to keep serving The three desire to continue bringing souls to Christ. He knows their hearts and speaks of their continuing service and the fullness of joy to come. 3 Nephi 28:1–12 3 Nephi 28:1-12 records Jesus asking His disciples what they desire. Nine ask to return to Him after their ministry; three desire to continue bringing souls to Him. He knows their hearts and promises joy in His Father's kingdom. Their exceptional callings are not a description of everyone's mortal experience. The conversation invites us to consider how hope for eternal life can deepen our desire to love and serve now. The pictures give visible settings to these recorded encounters. Clothing, architecture, and the physical form of the record are artistic interpretations; the linked passages provide the account we study. Watch these moments and return to the text These Church video excerpts dramatize the scriptural accounts. Notice the personal invitation and compassion in each scene, then return to the verses to distinguish the recorded witness from the production's visual interpretation. Book of Mormon video excerpt Jesus Christ Appears at the Temple | 3 Nephi 11:1–17 The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The people gathered at Bountiful hear the Father introduce His Son and witness the risen Savior come among them. Read His invitation to approach and know Him in 3 Nephi 11:14-17 . Book of Mormon video excerpt Jesus Christ Prays and Angels Minister to the Children | 3 Nephi 17:11–25 The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints This scene follows the Savior’s prayer and His care for the children. Return to 3 Nephi 17:11-25 to read how He blessed them one by one and how angels ministered to them. Read the witnesses together Compare the invitation to the multitude with Jesus' invitation to His disciples in Luke 24:36-43 . What do both accounts teach about His resurrected body? Then consider which part of His ministry in this section helps you trust His character. Keep your observation separate from questions the accounts do not answer. Mercy, agency, and our eternal future Resurrection, Judgment, and Eternal Life Living forever and receiving eternal life are related teachings with different meanings. Resurrection reunites body and spirit in immortality. Eternal life is life with God and the kind of life He lives, made possible through Jesus Christ. The Church study guide on eternal life explains this distinction. In John 17:3 , Jesus connects eternal life with knowing the Father and Himself. Judgment is God's work. Doctrine and Covenants 137:7-9 addresses people who died without knowledge of the gospel and teaches that the Lord considers both works and the desires of the heart. His knowledge of a person reaches beyond what family, neighbors, or observers can see. These verses invite trust in His justice and mercy, rather than conclusions about another person's eternal destiny. Explore and study Bring questions to the reading together Three generations gather around the resurrection account and listen to one another. Shared hope in the risen Christ can hold both testimony and honest questions. Read John 20 Latter-day Saints also believe that family relationships can endure through the Savior and temple covenants. That hope belongs within God's loving plan and respects each person's agency. The families and eternity study develops these promises with attention to the questions real families carry. What do the kingdoms of glory teach us? The restored gospel describes different kingdoms of glory and invites every person to come to Christ. President Oaks discusses these teachings in relation to our desires, choices, repentance, and the people we become. His message helps distinguish the gift of resurrection from exaltation with God. Read it as an invitation to follow the Savior. It does not give us a way to assign other people to a kingdom. General conference video and text Kingdoms of Glory The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2023 President Oaks teaches about the celestial, terrestrial, and telestial kingdoms. He connects final judgment with our choices and what we become through Jesus Christ, repentance, and covenant faithfulness. Pause and reflect: leave judgment with the Lord What do these teachings tell you about God's understanding of His children? What remains unknown to you? Consider a way to speak of someone who has died that honors their life and leaves final judgment with the Savior. Hope that reaches into today Walk with Christ While You Wait On the way to Emmaus, two disciples speak of the death of Jesus and their disappointed hopes. In Luke 24:13-32 , He walks with them, opens the scriptures, and is recognized as He breaks bread at their table. Their understanding grows through His presence and teaching. Explore and study Known in the breaking of bread The disciples recognize the risen Lord as He breaks bread. Their conversation returns to the scriptures He had opened along the road. Luke 24:28–35 For our own study, this account offers a gentle invitation: keep turning to Christ in scripture, prayer, and the company of people who will listen. It does not promise a particular spiritual experience on demand. You can take a small next step even when understanding comes slowly. Explore and study Hold hope and remembrance together A grandmother shares a keepsake and memory with her grandson. Remembering someone who has died can hold present sorrow beside hope in Christ's Resurrection. 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 If you are reading while grieving You may understand the doctrine and still feel someone's absence intensely. There is room for both. A familiar story, an ordinary meal, or a remembered kindness can carry love through a difficult day. You need not hurry past sorrow to prove that you believe. Mosiah 18:8-10 places bearing burdens, mourning together, and offering comfort within the covenant to follow God. When you support someone in grief, ask what would help, listen without pressing for a lesson, and offer practical care you can continue. You do not need to explain why their loved one died. Explore and study Let hope become a kindness A neighbor tends a small herb garden for someone who needs help. Such quiet service gives present purpose to Paul's promise that faithful labor in the Lord is not in vain. Read 1 Corinthians 15:58 Use the time we have today In Doors of Death , Elder Russell M. Nelson discusses physical death, the spirit world, resurrection, and judgment. His invitation to care more generously for others brings the study back to the time we have today. Paul closes his teaching about resurrection with a call to faithful labor in 1 Corinthians 15:58 . Hope in the risen Savior can become a visit, a meal, a remembered name, or steady companionship. General conference video and text Doors of Death The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 1992 Moroni 7:41-48 connects hope in Christ's Atonement and Resurrection with faith and charity. Consider one person you can care for this week, including yourself. The next step can be small and sincere. A simple way to study this week Read: choose one linked passage and read the surrounding verses. Remember: write one thing it teaches about Jesus Christ and one question you still carry. Care: choose one act of kindness or invite someone you trust to sit and read with you. The living Savior and the life before us Hope in Christ in Our Personal Circumstances The following five pictures are devotional interpretations that place the risen Christ beside people facing familiar circumstances today. They invite reflection on His love and living ministry. They do not portray reported appearances or promise a particular outcome. Read them with the scriptures and with the real needs of people in your own life in mind. When a loved one's place is empty Explore and study Companionship in grief A keepsake rests in her hands as she turns toward Him. This devotional scene invites us to bring sorrow to Christ and to listen with care when another person mourns. Mosiah 18:8–9 A keepsake can bring gratitude and grief into the same moment. Christ's Resurrection lets us hope beyond death while we continue to miss someone now. Return to John 11:32-36 and notice His compassion among those who mourn. You can speak a loved one's name, preserve a memory, and let someone share your sorrow without finding an explanation for the loss. When illness changes the day Explore and study Presence during illness The treatment room is quiet as they look toward one another. Christ’s knowledge of pain can sustain faith alongside medical care and the help of people who stay near. Alma 7:11–13 Alma 7:11-13 teaches that the Savior takes upon Himself pains, sicknesses, death, and infirmities, and knows how to help His people. The hope of resurrection is especially personal when the body is vulnerable. Prayer, medical care, and the help of loved ones can belong in the same day; needing treatment does not diminish faith. When loneliness makes life feel smaller Explore and study A conversation on the bench A shared bench becomes a place to speak and be heard. Hope in Christ can move us to notice someone, make time, and offer dependable companionship. Matthew 25:35–40 After a death or a difficult change, familiar routines can become quiet. The individual attention in 3 Nephi 11:14-17 invites reflection on each person's worth to Christ. As a practical response, consider one person you might call, sit beside, or invite for a walk. A small connection can be a way to give or receive care today. When you are carrying someone else's needs Explore and study Rest for the caregiver She pauses at the kitchen table and meets His eyes. His invitation to come and find rest can accompany the practical help, rest, and support a caregiver needs. Matthew 11:28–30 Caregiving can include devotion, exhaustion, and questions about what lies ahead. In Matthew 11:28-30 , Jesus invites the weary to come to Him and learn of Him. You can bring both love and fatigue into prayer. Letting another person share a task or sit with you can be one way to receive the burden-bearing care taught in Mosiah 18:8-10 . When the future is uncertain Explore and study Hope when the way is unclear The work on the desk can wait for a moment of attentive conversation. Trust in Christ’s living hope can support a next faithful step when the future remains uncertain. 1 Peter 1:3–5 Work, responsibilities, and unanswered questions can narrow our attention to what might go wrong. Moroni 7:41-48 grounds enduring hope in Christ's Atonement and Resurrection, and joins that hope to charity. Your worth and eternal possibilities reach beyond one result. You can take the next honest step, seek wise help, and continue caring for others while an answer is still unknown. A reflection for your own circumstances Which scene feels nearest to your life today? Read its linked passage and name what it actually teaches about Jesus Christ. Then choose one small response: a prayer, an honest conversation, an offer of help, or a request for support. You do not need to resolve every question about eternity before receiving or giving love today. Read and watch with the scriptures open Official Sources and Further Study These Church messages develop different parts of the same study. Choose the question you want to explore and compare the teaching with the linked scriptures. Conference messages include personal experiences; you can read at your own pace. General conference video and text Our Father’s Glorious Plan The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2017 Drawing on his experience as a physician, Elder Clayton speaks about birth, death, and hope in Jesus Christ. He follows the journey from the spirit world to resurrection and judgment, testifying that every person will rise again. General conference video and text Trust in the Lord The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2019 President Oaks explains what scripture teaches about the spirit world and the work of salvation there. When questions remain unanswered, he counsels trust in the Lord and care in distinguishing revealed doctrine from speculation. Eternal Life: Gospel Study Guide explains immortality and life with God. Plan of Salvation: Gospel Study Guide places mortality and the life to come within God's plan. Salvation: Gospel Study Guide considers what Christ saves us from and our response to Him. Spirit World: Gospel Study Guide gathers teachings about the interval before resurrection. Where would you like to go next? Families and eternity Explore the hope of enduring relationships through Jesus Christ and temple covenants. Faith during trials Consider prayer, patient faith, and help for what you are facing today. When a child has died Read the promises concerning little children alongside a compassionate discussion of loss. Why temple service includes the dead Study proxy ordinances, agency, and the Savior's invitation to every generation. Ask about life after death Return to the beginning

records.text: The spirit continues to live What Happens Between Death and Resurrection? At death, body and spirit separate. Alma 40:11-14 describes spirits continuing to live while they await resurrection. Alma speaks of paradise as peace and rest for the righteous, and of a painful condition for the wicked. These are conditions in the spirit world, distinct from the final reunion of body and spirit. Explore and study Hope between death and resurrection In a quiet garden, an older man pauses over Alma's words about the life of the spirit after death. The promise of resurrection through Jesus Christ brings hope close to the memories he carries. Read Alma 40 Read on to Alma 40:21-23 . The body and spirit are to be reunited, and a person is brought before God. Keeping these teachings together helps us avoid treating the spirit world as the end of the story. The Church study guide on the spirit world offers further passages and questions for careful study. Christ's work reaches those who have died Doctrine and Covenants 138:12-19 describes faithful spirits awaiting the Savior's arrival and the redemption He makes possible. The vision then explains how His message reaches others: in Doctrine and Covenants 138:29-35 , Christ commissions messengers from among the righteous to teach those in darkness. They teach faith, repentance, and the ordinances of the gospel. The vision does not describe salvation as automatic. Doctrine and Covenants 138:58-59 connects redemption with repentance and the ordinances of God's house. Latter-day Saints perform proxy ordinances in temples because those who have died cannot perform these earthly ordinances for themselves. Each person remains free to accept or reject what is offered. Continue with the temple study to explore that connection. General conference video and text The Redemption of the Dead and the Testimony of Jesus The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2000 Elder Christofferson explains how temple service bears witness of Christ’s Resurrection and the reach of His Atonement. He makes clear that people who have died retain their agency: proxy ordinances take effect only if they accept them. General conference video and text The Vision of the Redemption of the Dead The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2018 President Ballard recalls the losses Joseph F. Smith endured and invites us to study the revelation he received. Doctrine and Covenants 138:29-35 describes Christ commissioning messengers to carry His gospel to the dead. Pause and reflect: hope with humility Find what the vision says Christ and His messengers do. Then separate those teachings from questions it does not answer about a loved one's daily experience. We can trust God's care without claiming to know where a particular person is or what they are doing.

records.title: Everyone Will Be Resurrected
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Christ's victory over physical death Everyone Will Be Resurrected When the risen Jesus comes among His disciples in Luke 24:36-43 , He offers peace and invites them to see His hands and feet. He distinguishes His resurrected body from a spirit and eats in their presence. Resurrection is more than the continued life of the spirit after death. Explore and study Peace among the disciples Christ comes among His disciples and offers peace. His hands and His presence testify that the One they mourned is alive. John 20:19–23 Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 that Christ's Resurrection makes resurrection possible for all. Later, in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 and 1 Corinthians 15:51-57 , he describes mortality giving way to immortality and gives thanks to God for victory through Jesus Christ. This universal gift is not something we earn by being strong enough or by grieving in a particular way. Thomas and the witness we receive Explore and study An invitation to Thomas The Savior invites Thomas to witness for himself. John records Thomas’s answer of faith and Christ’s blessing on those who believe without seeing. John 20:24–29 Thomas was absent when Jesus first appeared to the assembled disciples. In John 20:24-29 , Jesus later invites Thomas to behold His hands and believe. The account also speaks to readers who have not seen Him. John explains his purpose in John 20:30-31 : his written witness invites belief in Jesus Christ and life through His name. Questions about resurrection can be brought to these witnesses patiently. Consider what they testify that Jesus did, then what His living reality means for the person you miss. Hope does not require you to invent details that scripture has not supplied.

records.title: Jesus Christ Ministers in the Book of Mormon
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Another witness of the risen Savior Jesus Christ Ministers in the Book of Mormon The Book of Mormon adds its witness of the same risen Jesus. 3 Nephi 11:1-12 places a multitude near the temple in Bountiful, where the Father introduces His Son and Jesus declares His identity and saving mission. The people encounter the Savior who has overcome death. His ministry among them shows the compassion of the One in whom their eternal hope rests. One by one, they come to Him Explore and study One by one One person steps forward while others wait. The account gives each witness a place in the multitude’s testimony that Jesus Christ has risen. 3 Nephi 11:14–17 In 3 Nephi 11:14-17 , Jesus invites the people to feel the marks in His hands, feet, and side. They approach individually and become witnesses of His living reality. Read this beside the New Testament witnesses: the Resurrection is the foundation of their worship and hope. Notice the time given to each person in a large multitude. As a reflection, consider the difference between knowing that Christ loves humanity and trusting that you matter to Him personally. He teaches a life shaped by mercy Explore and study Blessed are the merciful The risen Savior teaches mercy, purity of heart, and peacemaking. His victory over death also calls His followers into a life shaped by His love. 3 Nephi 12:3–9 The risen Lord's teaching includes comfort for those who mourn and blessings for the merciful, pure in heart, and peacemakers. Read 3 Nephi 12:3-9 slowly. His invitation joins hope for God's kingdom with the kind of people we are becoming now. Choose one of these teachings to carry into an ordinary relationship. A merciful response, a patient conversation, or a sincere effort toward peace can be part of discipleship while we look forward to life with God. He receives the sick and afflicted Explore and study He healed them every one Christ invites the people to bring those who are afflicted. The scripture records His compassion and the healing of every person brought to Him. 3 Nephi 17:5–10 3 Nephi 17:7-10 records the people bringing those who are sick or afflicted to Jesus, and His healing them. His compassion reaches those who suffer and the people who help them come. The account witnesses His power and mercy; it does not give a timetable for every healing we seek today. He kneels and prays for them Explore and study He prayed for them Jesus kneels and prays to the Father. The witnesses describe their joy, while leaving the full words of His prayer unrecorded. 3 Nephi 17:12–20 In 3 Nephi 17:15-20 , Jesus kneels upon the earth and prays to the Father. The witnesses describe joy beyond their ability to express. The prayer's full words are not recorded, so we let their witness stand without supplying a speech for Him. He blesses the children individually Explore and study A blessing for each child The children receive His attention one by one. Read the whole passage to follow the blessing and the angels’ ministry that comes afterward. 3 Nephi 17:21–24 3 Nephi 17:21-24 describes Jesus weeping, blessing little children one by one, and praying for them. The people then see angels minister to the children. This tender scene gives us another view of the risen Lord's love. It describes His ministry to living children, rather than a detailed picture of a child's experience after death. If you are mourning a child, you can linger with the Savior's care here and continue to the study on child loss for the specific promises about little children. He gives bread and fills their souls Explore and study He gives bread and fills their souls Christ gives bread to His disciples and directs them to share it. The people stand, receive the bread and wine, and are filled with the Spirit. 3 Nephi 20:1–9 In 3 Nephi 20:1-9 , Jesus directs the people to stand, breaks and blesses bread, and gives it to His disciples to share. He also gives wine and teaches the meaning of partaking. The people receive the Spirit and glorify Him. Remembering the living Savior draws their worship toward the One who gives lasting life. He asks that the resurrection witness be recorded Explore and study Preserving the resurrection witness Christ asks about the missing account of saints who rose and ministered. Nephi remembers, and the record is completed so this witness can be preserved. 3 Nephi 23:6–14 When Nephi brings the record in 3 Nephi 23:6-14 , Jesus asks about the fulfillment of Samuel's prophecy that saints would rise and minister to many. The disciples confirm that it happened, and the missing account is written. This moment connects careful recordkeeping with testimony of Christ's victory over death. The witness matters enough to preserve for those who will read later. He listens to the disciples' desires Explore and study The desire to keep serving The three desire to continue bringing souls to Christ. He knows their hearts and speaks of their continuing service and the fullness of joy to come. 3 Nephi 28:1–12 3 Nephi 28:1-12 records Jesus asking His disciples what they desire. Nine ask to return to Him after their ministry; three desire to continue bringing souls to Him. He knows their hearts and promises joy in His Father's kingdom. Their exceptional callings are not a description of everyone's mortal experience. The conversation invites us to consider how hope for eternal life can deepen our desire to love and serve now. The pictures give visible settings to these recorded encounters. Clothing, architecture, and the physical form of the record are artistic interpretations; the linked passages provide the account we study. Watch these moments and return to the text These Church video excerpts dramatize the scriptural accounts. Notice the personal invitation and compassion in each scene, then return to the verses to distinguish the recorded witness from the production's visual interpretation. Book of Mormon video excerpt Jesus Christ Appears at the Temple | 3 Nephi 11:1–17 The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The people gathered at Bountiful hear the Father introduce His Son and witness the risen Savior come among them. Read His invitation to approach and know Him in 3 Nephi 11:14-17 . Book of Mormon video excerpt Jesus Christ Prays and Angels Minister to the Children | 3 Nephi 17:11–25 The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints This scene follows the Savior’s prayer and His care for the children. Return to 3 Nephi 17:11-25 to read how He blessed them one by one and how angels ministered to them. Read the witnesses together Compare the invitation to the multitude with Jesus' invitation to His disciples in Luke 24:36-43 . What do both accounts teach about His resurrected body? Then consider which part of His ministry in this section helps you trust His character. Keep your observation separate from questions the accounts do not answer.

records.title: Resurrection, Judgment, and Eternal Life
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Mercy, agency, and our eternal future Resurrection, Judgment, and Eternal Life Living forever and receiving eternal life are related teachings with different meanings. Resurrection reunites body and spirit in immortality. Eternal life is life with God and the kind of life He lives, made possible through Jesus Christ. The Church study guide on eternal life explains this distinction. In John 17:3 , Jesus connects eternal life with knowing the Father and Himself. Judgment is God's work. Doctrine and Covenants 137:7-9 addresses people who died without knowledge of the gospel and teaches that the Lord considers both works and the desires of the heart. His knowledge of a person reaches beyond what family, neighbors, or observers can see. These verses invite trust in His justice and mercy, rather than conclusions about another person's eternal destiny. Explore and study Bring questions to the reading together Three generations gather around the resurrection account and listen to one another. Shared hope in the risen Christ can hold both testimony and honest questions. Read John 20 Latter-day Saints also believe that family relationships can endure through the Savior and temple covenants. That hope belongs within God's loving plan and respects each person's agency. The families and eternity study develops these promises with attention to the questions real families carry. What do the kingdoms of glory teach us? The restored gospel describes different kingdoms of glory and invites every person to come to Christ. President Oaks discusses these teachings in relation to our desires, choices, repentance, and the people we become. His message helps distinguish the gift of resurrection from exaltation with God. Read it as an invitation to follow the Savior. It does not give us a way to assign other people to a kingdom. General conference video and text Kingdoms of Glory The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2023 President Oaks teaches about the celestial, terrestrial, and telestial kingdoms. He connects final judgment with our choices and what we become through Jesus Christ, repentance, and covenant faithfulness. Pause and reflect: leave judgment with the Lord What do these teachings tell you about God's understanding of His children? What remains unknown to you? Consider a way to speak of someone who has died that honors their life and leaves final judgment with the Savior.

records.title: Walk with Christ While You Wait
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Hope that reaches into today Walk with Christ While You Wait On the way to Emmaus, two disciples speak of the death of Jesus and their disappointed hopes. In Luke 24:13-32 , He walks with them, opens the scriptures, and is recognized as He breaks bread at their table. Their understanding grows through His presence and teaching. Explore and study Known in the breaking of bread The disciples recognize the risen Lord as He breaks bread. Their conversation returns to the scriptures He had opened along the road. Luke 24:28–35 For our own study, this account offers a gentle invitation: keep turning to Christ in scripture, prayer, and the company of people who will listen. It does not promise a particular spiritual experience on demand. You can take a small next step even when understanding comes slowly. Explore and study Hold hope and remembrance together A grandmother shares a keepsake and memory with her grandson. Remembering someone who has died can hold present sorrow beside hope in Christ's Resurrection. 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 If you are reading while grieving You may understand the doctrine and still feel someone's absence intensely. There is room for both. A familiar story, an ordinary meal, or a remembered kindness can carry love through a difficult day. You need not hurry past sorrow to prove that you believe. Mosiah 18:8-10 places bearing burdens, mourning together, and offering comfort within the covenant to follow God. When you support someone in grief, ask what would help, listen without pressing for a lesson, and offer practical care you can continue. You do not need to explain why their loved one died. Explore and study Let hope become a kindness A neighbor tends a small herb garden for someone who needs help. Such quiet service gives present purpose to Paul's promise that faithful labor in the Lord is not in vain. Read 1 Corinthians 15:58 Use the time we have today In Doors of Death , Elder Russell M. Nelson discusses physical death, the spirit world, resurrection, and judgment. His invitation to care more generously for others brings the study back to the time we have today. Paul closes his teaching about resurrection with a call to faithful labor in 1 Corinthians 15:58 . Hope in the risen Savior can become a visit, a meal, a remembered name, or steady companionship. General conference video and text Doors of Death The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 1992 Moroni 7:41-48 connects hope in Christ's Atonement and Resurrection with faith and charity. Consider one person you can care for this week, including yourself. The next step can be small and sincere. A simple way to study this week Read: choose one linked passage and read the surrounding verses. Remember: write one thing it teaches about Jesus Christ and one question you still carry. Care: choose one act of kindness or invite someone you trust to sit and read with you.

records.title: Hope in Christ in Our Personal Circumstances
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: The living Savior and the life before us Hope in Christ in Our Personal Circumstances The following five pictures are devotional interpretations that place the risen Christ beside people facing familiar circumstances today. They invite reflection on His love and living ministry. They do not portray reported appearances or promise a particular outcome. Read them with the scriptures and with the real needs of people in your own life in mind. When a loved one's place is empty Explore and study Companionship in grief A keepsake rests in her hands as she turns toward Him. This devotional scene invites us to bring sorrow to Christ and to listen with care when another person mourns. Mosiah 18:8–9 A keepsake can bring gratitude and grief into the same moment. Christ's Resurrection lets us hope beyond death while we continue to miss someone now. Return to John 11:32-36 and notice His compassion among those who mourn. You can speak a loved one's name, preserve a memory, and let someone share your sorrow without finding an explanation for the loss. When illness changes the day Explore and study Presence during illness The treatment room is quiet as they look toward one another. Christ’s knowledge of pain can sustain faith alongside medical care and the help of people who stay near. Alma 7:11–13 Alma 7:11-13 teaches that the Savior takes upon Himself pains, sicknesses, death, and infirmities, and knows how to help His people. The hope of resurrection is especially personal when the body is vulnerable. Prayer, medical care, and the help of loved ones can belong in the same day; needing treatment does not diminish faith. When loneliness makes life feel smaller Explore and study A conversation on the bench A shared bench becomes a place to speak and be heard. Hope in Christ can move us to notice someone, make time, and offer dependable companionship. Matthew 25:35–40 After a death or a difficult change, familiar routines can become quiet. The individual attention in 3 Nephi 11:14-17 invites reflection on each person's worth to Christ. As a practical response, consider one person you might call, sit beside, or invite for a walk. A small connection can be a way to give or receive care today. When you are carrying someone else's needs Explore and study Rest for the caregiver She pauses at the kitchen table and meets His eyes. His invitation to come and find rest can accompany the practical help, rest, and support a caregiver needs. Matthew 11:28–30 Caregiving can include devotion, exhaustion, and questions about what lies ahead. In Matthew 11:28-30 , Jesus invites the weary to come to Him and learn of Him. You can bring both love and fatigue into prayer. Letting another person share a task or sit with you can be one way to receive the burden-bearing care taught in Mosiah 18:8-10 . When the future is uncertain Explore and study Hope when the way is unclear The work on the desk can wait for a moment of attentive conversation. Trust in Christ’s living hope can support a next faithful step when the future remains uncertain. 1 Peter 1:3–5 Work, responsibilities, and unanswered questions can narrow our attention to what might go wrong. Moroni 7:41-48 grounds enduring hope in Christ's Atonement and Resurrection, and joins that hope to charity. Your worth and eternal possibilities reach beyond one result. You can take the next honest step, seek wise help, and continue caring for others while an answer is still unknown. A reflection for your own circumstances Which scene feels nearest to your life today? Read its linked passage and name what it actually teaches about Jesus Christ. Then choose one small response: a prayer, an honest conversation, an offer of help, or a request for support. You do not need to resolve every question about eternity before receiving or giving love today.

records.title: Official Sources and Further Study
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Read and watch with the scriptures open Official Sources and Further Study These Church messages develop different parts of the same study. Choose the question you want to explore and compare the teaching with the linked scriptures. Conference messages include personal experiences; you can read at your own pace. General conference video and text Our Father’s Glorious Plan The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2017 Drawing on his experience as a physician, Elder Clayton speaks about birth, death, and hope in Jesus Christ. He follows the journey from the spirit world to resurrection and judgment, testifying that every person will rise again. General conference video and text Trust in the Lord The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2019 President Oaks explains what scripture teaches about the spirit world and the work of salvation there. When questions remain unanswered, he counsels trust in the Lord and care in distinguishing revealed doctrine from speculation. Eternal Life: Gospel Study Guide explains immortality and life with God. Plan of Salvation: Gospel Study Guide places mortality and the life to come within God's plan. Salvation: Gospel Study Guide considers what Christ saves us from and our response to Him. Spirit World: Gospel Study Guide gathers teachings about the interval before resurrection.

records.title: Where would you like to go next?
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Families and eternity Explore the hope of enduring relationships through Jesus Christ and temple covenants. Faith during trials Consider prayer, patient faith, and help for what you are facing today. When a child has died Read the promises concerning little children alongside a compassionate discussion of loss. Why temple service includes the dead Study proxy ordinances, agency, and the Savior's invitation to every generation. Ask about life after death Return to the beginning

records.title: What Is Eternal Marriage?
records.text: Answers / Eternal marriage Latter-day Saints believe a husband and wife may be sealed in a temple by priesthood authority so their marriage can continue after death. The ceremony is sacred, but eternal marriage is more than a single day: it is a covenant life of faith in Jesus Christ, repentance, loyalty, service, and love. This teaching can touch deep hopes and deep wounds. Marital status does not measure a person’s worth or place in the Church. Covenants never require anyone to remain in danger or tolerate abuse. Christ at the center A sealing begins a covenant journey Jesus taught that God intends marriage to be a union, not a contest for power. Latter-day Saint teaching adds that the sealing authority Christ described can bind on earth and in heaven. In the temple, spouses covenant with God and with one another. Those promises are made possible through Jesus Christ and become a daily invitation to follow His way. Eternal does not mean that an unhealthy pattern should simply last forever. A Christ-centered marriage grows through agency, humility, equal counsel, forgiveness, fidelity, tenderness, and truth. Both spouses remain responsible for their own choices, and God’s judgment is perfectly just and merciful. Marriage through time One gospel ideal, lived in many circumstances These scenes move from Eden to the present, showing couples and families learning covenant love across different eras and circumstances. In every scene, Jesus Christ is the Savior and Teacher who calls His disciples to covenant love, equal partnership, fidelity, and mercy. 01 · Eden The beginning: companionship and shared stewardship Latter-day Saints read Adam and Eve’s union as marriage established by God. Their story begins with companionship, cleaving to one another, and becoming one while each remains a moral agent. Read Moses 3:18–24 02 · Ancient home Covenant character grows in ordinary life A lasting marriage is shaped in daily choices: loyalty, honest work, hospitality, patience, and care. The setting is symbolic; the principle is that sacred promises are lived at home. Read Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 03 · The Savior’s world Christ teaches unity without domination Jesus pointed marriage back to God’s intention that husband and wife become one. His gospel also rejects control and invites both disciples to lead through service, truth, repentance, and love. Read Matthew 19:4–6 04 · Restoration Sealing hope returns Latter-day Saints believe Elijah restored sealing keys in the Kirtland Temple. That authority joins family hope to Jesus Christ’s power over death and asks covenant keepers to live faithfully now. Read Doctrine and Covenants 110:13–16 05 · Dignity and belonging Divine worth is never a marital ranking A temple sealing is sacred in Latter-day Saint belief, but it is not a measure of human worth. People who are civilly married, single, divorced, widowed, in an interfaith family, or not yet sealed deserve full dignity, welcome, and Christlike care. Study belonging in the Church 06 · Today and onward A covenant journey, not a perfect photograph Temple sealing begins a life of discipleship. Husband and wife walk side by side as equal partners, relying on the Savior’s grace and choosing again and again to counsel, repent, forgive, protect, and serve. Study equal partnership with Elder Soares Every person is of infinite worth. Marriage and sealing status describe circumstances and covenants. They do not establish a hierarchy of souls. Jesus Christ’s invitation to come unto Him is extended to all. A scripture path Trace the doctrine, then bring it home Read one passage at a time. Ask what it teaches about God, covenant, agency, and the way two disciples should treat each other. Matthew 16:19 Christ speaks of authority to bind on earth and in heaven. Moses 3:18, 21–24 Companionship and becoming one without erasing either person. Doctrine and Covenants 42:22 Wholehearted marital loyalty. Doctrine and Covenants 131:1–4 Eternal marriage in the doctrine of exaltation. Doctrine and Covenants 132:19 Sealing, covenant conditions, and the Holy Spirit of Promise. Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–46 Influence through persuasion, gentleness, love, and integrity, without compulsion. Moroni 7:45–48 Charity as a gift from Christ and a daily way of loving. John 17:20–23 Unity patterned after the Father and the Son. A context note: Doctrine and Covenants 132 addresses more than marriage and includes historical questions about plural marriage. Read verse 19 in its full section and use the official sources below rather than making it carry every question by itself. Four voices, four study questions Watch, read, and reflect Conference talk · October 2008 Celestial Marriage President Russell M. Nelson explains temple marriage, individual discipleship, and covenant faithfulness. Ask: What makes Christ a partner in an eternal marriage? Russell M. Nelson Conference talk · April 2013 Marriage: Watch and Learn Elder L. Whitney Clayton describes commitment, faith, repentance, humility, respect, loyalty, and love. Ask: Which quiet habit would bring more light into a relationship? L. Whitney Clayton Conference talk · October 2022 In Partnership with the Lord Elder Ulisses Soares teaches full and equal partnership, walking side by side with Christ. Ask: Where could counsel replace control? Ulisses Soares Conference talk · April 2024 Fruit That Remains Elder Matthew L. Carpenter carefully distinguishes the covenant with God, the bond between spouses, personal faithfulness, and agency. Ask: What hope does God’s perfect justice offer? Matthew L. Carpenter Newest conference study: Eternal Marriage Is an Eternal Journey, Elder Neil L. Andersen, April 2026 Questions people carry Clear answers with room for individual circumstances Is a temple wedding automatically eternal? No. The sealing ordinance opens eternal promises, but scripture connects those promises with covenant faithfulness and ratification by the Holy Spirit of Promise. A ceremony should not be treated as a guarantee that makes choices or agency irrelevant. What is different from a civil marriage? A civil marriage establishes a legal union. A temple sealing is a priesthood ordinance in which husband and wife make sacred covenants with God and each other, with promises that can extend beyond death. Legal requirements still matter, and local practice varies. What if one spouse stops believing or breaks covenants? Each person retains agency and answers to God for individual choices. A faithful person is not mechanically stripped of every promised blessing by another person’s decisions. God will not force an unwilling or unworthy relationship to continue eternally, and individual outcomes belong to His perfect judgment. What about someone who is single, divorced, or widowed? They fully belong now. Church teaching promises every blessing of exaltation to faithful covenant keepers, but it is wise not to speculate about when, how, or with whom an individual promise will be fulfilled. Present marital status is not a spiritual ranking. Does forgiveness mean remaining in an unsafe marriage? No. Covenant language never requires tolerating abuse. Forgiveness, legal decisions, personal safety, Church membership, and the future of a marriage are related but distinct questions. Seek immediate safety and qualified local help when harm or threats are present. How can Christ be at the center today? Pray and worship together when both are willing; listen without preparing a defense; repent for your own conduct; share decisions; keep confidences and promises; serve in small ways; and invite help early. One spouse cannot do the agency-work of the other. A seven-day study pattern Move from doctrine to discipleship Authority Read Matthew 16:19 . Write what Christ’s sealing authority means to you. Covenant Read D&C 131:1–4 and 132:19 in context. Note every condition and promise. Charity Read Moroni 7:45–48 . Choose one quality to practice without keeping score. Equal partnership Watch Elder Soares. Ask where listening and shared counsel could deepen. Repentance Watch Elder Clayton. Name one change that belongs to you, not your spouse. Hope Read Elder Carpenter. Bring an unresolved sealing question to God without forcing an answer. Christ Read John 17:20–23 . Pray for unity founded in truth, love, and willing discipleship. A reflection to keep What does the Savior invite me to become in my closest relationships? Record one impression and one loving, safe action you can take. If you are studying alone, the same pattern can strengthen your preparation, healing, family relationships, and covenant discipleship. Official sources and further study Marriage: Gospel Study Guide What Happens in a Temple Sealing? Single Members of the Church In Crisis? Talk Now: Help for Victims of Abuse Ask a Question Families and Belonging Why Temples? Where would you like to go next? Build belonging in every family circumstance Continue from eternal marriage into divine identity, care, parenting, and family hope. When marriage includes separation or divorce Study dignity, boundaries, grief, faith, and support without an idealized story. Place eternal relationships beside Resurrection Explore the spirit world, universal resurrection through Christ, judgment, and eternal life.

records.title: Clear answers with room for individual circumstances
records.text: Questions people carry Clear answers with room for individual circumstances Is a temple wedding automatically eternal? No. The sealing ordinance opens eternal promises, but scripture connects those promises with covenant faithfulness and ratification by the Holy Spirit of Promise. A ceremony should not be treated as a guarantee that makes choices or agency irrelevant. What is different from a civil marriage? A civil marriage establishes a legal union. A temple sealing is a priesthood ordinance in which husband and wife make sacred covenants with God and each other, with promises that can extend beyond death. Legal requirements still matter, and local practice varies. What if one spouse stops believing or breaks covenants? Each person retains agency and answers to God for individual choices. A faithful person is not mechanically stripped of every promised blessing by another person’s decisions. God will not force an unwilling or unworthy relationship to continue eternally, and individual outcomes belong to His perfect judgment. What about someone who is single, divorced, or widowed? They fully belong now. Church teaching promises every blessing of exaltation to faithful covenant keepers, but it is wise not to speculate about when, how, or with whom an individual promise will be fulfilled. Present marital status is not a spiritual ranking. Does forgiveness mean remaining in an unsafe marriage? No. Covenant language never requires tolerating abuse. Forgiveness, legal decisions, personal safety, Church membership, and the future of a marriage are related but distinct questions. Seek immediate safety and qualified local help when harm or threats are present. How can Christ be at the center today? Pray and worship together when both are willing; listen without preparing a defense; repent for your own conduct; share decisions; keep confidences and promises; serve in small ways; and invite help early. One spouse cannot do the agency-work of the other.

records.title: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.keywords: what is the book of mormon
records.text: Answers / Book of Mormon Latter-day Saints accept the Book of Mormon as scripture and call it “Another Testament of Jesus Christ.” They do not see it as a replacement for the Bible, but as an additional witness of the Savior and His gospel. Follow the record Explore Book of Mormon Evidences Study the translation, Royal Skousen’s manuscript research, witness accounts, chiasmus, stylometry, and ancient context. Follow original sources, consider sincere questions, and return to the book’s witness of Jesus Christ. Explore the Evidences Study Begin with the Translation This is an independent Latter-day Saint study page. Official Church resources are linked for verification and further reading. Watch and study An Introduction Before You Begin Reading The official short explainer What Is the Book of Mormon? introduces the record, its setting, and its witness of Jesus Christ. Watch for the question that matters most to you: what the book contains, why Latter-day Saints read it, or how it relates to the Savior. Church video What Is the Book of Mormon? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Then begin with the people gathered at Bountiful in 3 Nephi 11:1-17 . They hear a voice, turn their attention toward heaven, and encounter Jesus Christ. His introduction connects His identity with His suffering for the sins of the world. The people are invited to approach Him individually. How does reading this account add to the overview you just watched? What the Book Claims to Be The Book of Mormon presents itself as an ancient record of peoples in the Americas, written and abridged by prophets and translated by Joseph Smith through the gift and power of God. Its stated purpose is to persuade readers that Jesus is the Christ and to invite them to come unto Him. Why It Is Called Another Testament of Jesus Christ The book contains prophecies of Christ before His birth, teachings about His Atonement and Resurrection, and an account of the resurrected Savior appearing to people in the Americas. Jesus Christ is therefore not a side subject in the book; He is its central witness. Does It Replace the Bible? No. Latter-day Saints study the Old and New Testaments as scripture and cherish the Bible’s witness of Jesus Christ. The Book of Mormon is understood as a second scriptural witness that supports biblical teachings and can clarify or reinforce doctrines such as faith, repentance, baptism, resurrection, grace, and discipleship. Why Have More Than One Scriptural Witness? The Bible itself uses the principle that important truth can be established by multiple witnesses. Latter-day Saints see the Bible and Book of Mormon as separate records that converge on Jesus Christ. Their different histories and settings make the shared witness meaningful rather than redundant. How a Seeker Can Approach It The Church invites people to read the Book of Mormon, compare its teachings with the Bible, ponder its message, and pray for spiritual confirmation. The point is not simply to learn facts about a new book, but to test whether its teachings lead a reader toward Jesus Christ. Try Reading One Account If the book is unfamiliar, 3 Nephi 11:1-17 is a useful starting point. It tells of the resurrected Jesus appearing to a gathered people and inviting them to come forward individually. Read at your own pace, note what stands out, and keep track of your questions. You can also explore a short comparison with a Bible passage . What Does the Invitation to Pray Include? Moroni 10:3-5 invites readers to remember God's mercy, ponder, and ask sincerely in the name of Christ. Reading and reflection are part of that invitation. It need not become a demand to report a dramatic feeling after a single reading. If you are uncertain, keep track of the passage or claim you want to understand. A conversation can be more helpful when you can point to the actual words. The prayer and revelation study discusses discernment and questions that take time. Watch and study Why Nephi Keeps Returning to Jesus Christ Explore and study Follow Nephi’s stated purpose A reader pauses over an open book above a green valley. Nephi's stated purpose gives the study its center: persuading people to believe in Jesus Christ and be reconciled to God. Read 2 Nephi 25 In 2 Nephi 25:23-29 , Nephi explains why he writes and teaches about Christ. His concern includes the next generation: he wants children to understand where forgiveness is found. Read the verbs in verse 26 , then read the invitation to worship in verse 29 . Study lesson 2 Nephi 25: Saved by Jesus Christ The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The accompanying Seminary lesson explores salvation through Jesus Christ. After reading it, put Nephi's purpose into your own words. How would a family conversation change if it helped someone understand the Savior's mercy? You can begin with one experience of gratitude or one sincere question. A polished religious speech is unnecessary. Get to Know the Book by Reading It Explore and study Come forward and know The risen Jesus Christ extends His invitation to people gathered at Bountiful. Each person is welcomed to come forward and know for themselves that He is the God of Israel. 3 Nephi 11:10-17 Study a teaching, not only the book's description Alma 32:21-28, 37-43 uses the image of a seed to discuss faith and the patient care that follows an initial willingness to believe. The setting includes people who have been excluded from worship because of their poverty. Notice both the invitation to begin and the warning that growth requires continued nourishment. This is a religious account of developing faith; it is not a scientific experiment that establishes every historical claim about the book. Read the gospel invitation 2 Nephi 31:5-13, 17-21 connects Jesus's example with baptism and an ongoing life of faith, hope, and love. Read this beside the account of His ministry in 3 Nephi 11 already linked above. One explains a path of discipleship; the other portrays an encounter with the risen Savior. Together they show why the book matters in Latter-day Saint worship. Separate the questions you are asking You may be asking what the book teaches, how it came into print, whether its account is historical, or how to evaluate a spiritual conviction. Those are related but different inquiries. Reading a passage can illuminate its message; historical questions require historical evidence too. Keep a question list so one unresolved issue does not get quietly replaced by another. A reading note you can return to Record a passage, its speaker and setting, one teaching in your own words, and one question. On your next visit, start with that question rather than feeling you must begin the whole book again. A First Journey Through Three Kinds of Passage Explore and study Pause and ponder the promise A woman pauses beside a quiet lake with an open book in her lap. The still water and unhurried posture echo Moroni's invitation to remember, ponder and ask God with faith in Christ. Moroni 10:3-5 These focusChrist study suggestions offer a way to explore the sources at your own pace. Explore and study Let the words settle in the heart A grandmother listens as a teenage boy shares what he has found in an open book. Together they read, ponder and speak of Christ, letting understanding grow through a patient conversation. Read 3 Nephi 17 Explore and study Read a covenant through acts of care Neighbors load food and folded blankets into a car, making the covenant to bear one another's burdens visible through ordinary care. Read Mosiah 18 1. Notice Christ's care for individuals Read 3 Nephi 17:1-9, 21 . Jesus recognizes that His listeners need time to understand. He invites pondering and prayer, responds with compassion to their tears, heals those brought to Him, and blesses children individually. Write down a detail you might miss in a quick reading. As a personal application, make room for someone who needs time, attention, or help. Let the account deepen your understanding of compassion without turning its healings into a timetable for your own circumstances. 2. Follow belief into a community Read Mosiah 18:7-10, 21-29 . Alma connects baptism with caring for people who mourn or carry burdens. The community is also taught to share according to its members' resources and needs. Consider how belonging to Christ affects ordinary relationships. Who could use company, practical help, or a patient listener? Choose a specific, freely offered act of care. The passage gives a picture of covenant life you can discuss even while other questions about the book remain open. 3. Keep an honest record of your reading Return to one passage already studied. Write four short notes: what happens, what is taught about Christ, what you want to understand, and what you might do. Keep the chapter reference beside your notes so you can check your impressions against the text. On another day, revisit the question that mattered most. You may want to read a surrounding chapter, compare a Bible passage, pray, or ask someone to study with you. An ongoing conversation with the text can begin before you feel ready to make a final judgment about every claim. Where should I go when my question is historical? Use the Book of Mormon text to understand its message, then name the historical claim you want to investigate. The Joseph Smith and Restoration study offers a route into the history. Keep textual interpretation, historical evidence, and personal spiritual conviction distinct in your notes. Official Sources and Further Study The Book of Mormon: Another Testament of Jesus Christ How the Bible and the Book of Mormon Work Together Read the Book of Mormon in Gospel Library Ask a Question How the Two Books Work Together Where would you like to go next? Read the two books together Try a focused comparison while preserving the context of each passage. Explore prayer and discernment Consider how study, prayer, agency, and uncertainty can belong in the same inquiry. See the Savior's ministry in 3 Nephi Pair official Book of Mormon films with their chapters and continue into Christ's care for individuals.
