records.title: Who Was Joseph Smith?
records.text: Answers / Joseph Smith Joseph Smith (1805-1844) was the founding prophet of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Latter-day Saints believe God called him to help restore the gospel and Church of Jesus Christ in the latter days. Stand Forever · Third foundational question Was Joseph Smith a prophet? Joseph Smith reported visions, brought forth the Book of Mormon, organized the Church in 1830, and taught doctrines that continue to shape Latter-day Saint faith. His prophetic claim can be examined through his firsthand accounts, contemporary records, the texts he presented as scripture, and the lasting fruits of his ministry. Explore and study Consider the work of publishing a book Two printers set type and prepare pages by hand for the Book of Mormon's 1830 publication. The press, ink and stacked paper reveal the patience and skilled labor required to place the finished book into a reader's hands. Book of Mormon introduction Begin with the accounts. Read the First Vision sources linked below. Notice who recorded each account, when it was recorded, and which question you are asking of it. Study a scriptural claim. Follow the Book of Mormon references and the Harmony study. Distinguish what a source claims from what a later interpretation adds. Continue the inquiry. Use the reviewed videos and reflection questions to identify a useful next source. Then explore the restored Church study for the beliefs, ordinances, and community connected with this history. Read the source accounts Watch and study The face behind the history. Explore an art-led companion study of Joseph’s death masks, portraits, and the likeness developed for focusChrist. Open the portrait story → Latter-day Saints regard Joseph Smith as a prophet called by God. The historical sources below distinguish his firsthand accounts, contemporary records, later recollections, and the Church’s interpretation of his life. Watch and study Begin in the grove, then open the records The film Joseph Smith: The Prophet of the Restoration offers a dramatic introduction to his life and legacy. Begin your examination with his reported First Vision. Watch with a source question in mind: what can you identify in the written accounts, and what belongs to a filmmaker's portrayal? Church video Joseph Smith: The Prophet of the Restoration The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The Church's First Vision Accounts essay identifies four firsthand accounts. Its discussion of the 1832 account emphasizes Joseph's concern for forgiveness and personal redemption. The 1838 account places the vision within the beginnings of the Church and emphasizes his question about which church to join. These are different dates of recording, not four dates for the event. Begin with one account, noting its audience and emphasis. Then compare a second. The essay presents the Church's explanation of differences and links to documents so that you can examine more than a modern summary. The First Vision Joseph Smith grew up during intense religious revival in the northeastern United States. As a teenager, he sought divine guidance about which church to join. He later recorded that in answer to prayer he saw God the Father and Jesus Christ. Latter-day Saints call this experience the First Vision and regard it as the beginning of the Restoration. The Book of Mormon Joseph said an angel named Moroni later directed him to an ancient record written on metal plates. He translated the record by the gift and power of God, and it was published in 1830 as the Book of Mormon. The book presents itself as another testament of Jesus Christ. The Restoration of the Church Latter-day Saints believe priesthood authority, gospel ordinances, prophetic revelation, and the organization of Christ’s Church were restored through Joseph Smith. The Church was formally organized in 1830. Joseph served as its first president and received revelations that now form a substantial portion of the Doctrine and Covenants. Joseph Smith Was Not the Object of Worship Latter-day Saints honor Joseph as a prophet, but worship God the Father in the name of Jesus Christ. Joseph’s prophetic role is meaningful to believers because they understand his mission as pointing people to Jesus Christ, restoring priesthood authority, and bringing forth scripture that testifies of Christ. A Historical Figure Worth Studying Carefully Joseph Smith’s life included religious leadership, migration, conflict, legal controversy, political activity, plural marriage, and violence directed both toward and around the early Saints. A responsible study should not reduce him to either a flawless hero or a caricature. The Church’s history resources include primary-source context and essays for difficult questions as well as devotional accounts. If a Historical Question Troubles You You can examine one question at a time. Begin with the linked accounts, notice when and why each was written, and distinguish what the record says from later interpretation. If you are discussing the question with someone else, make room for what it means to them as well as the evidence. You do not need to rush past a concern to keep learning. Follow a Historical Question to the Records The Church's First Vision Accounts essay discusses differences among the accounts and explains the Church's interpretation of them. Its notes provide a path to the underlying records. Read an account before its commentary when you can, and distinguish Joseph's reported experience from a historian's explanation of the record. A devotional account and a historical essay may serve different purposes. Asking when a text was written, who preserved it, and what evidence is available is a reasonable part of study. You can hold a specific question open while examining it carefully. A Worked Example: Studying the First Vision Read the account before the summary Joseph Smith History 1:5-20 recounts religious disagreement, Joseph's reading and prayer, and his reported vision. Record the questions he describes and the response he says he received. This is the scriptural account accepted by Latter-day Saints; identifying it as an account is important when studying history. Explore and study Joseph Smith's account in his own words A reader leans over Joseph Smith's written account with another book open beside it. Beginning with his own words lets the record speak before we decide what his life and testimony mean. Read Joseph Smith–History 1 Compare accounts with attention to when they were recorded Use the First Vision Accounts essay linked above to reach the other records. Compare emphasis, wording, audience, and date of recording. The date an event is said to have occurred and the date a surviving account was written are different facts. The essay offers the Church's interpretation of differences; the underlying documents allow you to examine the evidence yourself. Keep historical and spiritual questions distinct A historical investigation can ask what records survive and how they relate. A spiritual inquiry may ask what the Restoration claim means for belief and practice. Those inquiries can inform each other, but one should not silently stand in for the other. If a concern remains, name it specifically and pursue the relevant evidence. A useful source note Write the title, author or recorder, date of the record, and exact passage you are considering. Add a separate sentence for your interpretation. This keeps a later retelling from becoming indistinguishable from the original evidence. Watch and study From a personal inquiry to shared work Explore and study Joseph Smith's accounts across time A handwritten record lies open beside an inkwell on a nineteenth-century desk. Preserved across time, Joseph Smith's accounts let readers follow how he described his search for God in his own words. Joseph Smith History 1:5-20 Explore and study Oliver Cowdery joins the work Two readers place the revelation beside their notes, tracing the shared labor, uncertainty and reassurance surrounding Oliver Cowdery's work with Joseph Smith. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 In his October 2014 address Joseph Smith , Elder Neil L. Andersen discusses the Restoration and invites a personal witness through prayer and scripture. Compare his statement of faith with a revelation from the work surrounding the Book of Mormon. Read the heading to Doctrine and Covenants 6 as historical context. It identifies Harmony, Pennsylvania, April 1829, and Oliver Cowdery's work as a scribe beginning April 7. Church video Joseph Smith The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Verses 18-20 combine support with accountability. Oliver is asked to stand by Joseph in difficulty, and the two are to give and receive correction. Patience, faith, hope, and charity belong within that relationship. This is a useful passage to keep beside a history of religious leadership because the text itself makes room for faults and growth. In verses 21-23 the speaker identifies Himself as Jesus Christ and recalls peace given to Oliver. In verses 36-37 attention turns again to Christ and His wounds. Consider how the revelation directs a participant in the Restoration toward the Savior. Continue that connection in the full D&C 6:36 study . A study you can carry into the week These focusChrist prompts are invitations for personal reflection. Explore and study Bring the question to God A man bows his head beside a closed book on a quiet park bench, giving prayer and careful study room to work together as he seeks understanding. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 First session: establish the question Choose a single question about Joseph's life. Write it in language that a source could help answer: what did he report, when was it recorded, or how did a particular teaching develop? Avoid making one question stand for his entire life. Second session: follow a citation Open a document linked from the First Vision essay. Read the surrounding passage. Note the recorder, recording date, and what the document actually says. If your question concerns a different period, use the Church History section to find the relevant sources. Third session: assess the interpretation Write a short account of what you learned, separating evidence from your explanation of it. Name any remaining uncertainty. A source can establish what a witness reported without resolving every question about the experience being described. Fourth session: consider the spiritual claim Read D&C 6 with the historical questions still clearly named. What does its invitation to seek wisdom, accept correction, and look to Christ mean for your own conduct? Personal reflection can accompany careful investigation without replacing it. Bring a passage and a specific question to Ask , then check the response against the linked original sources. Official Sources and Further Study Joseph Smith and the Restoration: Church Newsroom Joseph Smith’s First Vision Accounts Joseph Smith History Joseph Smith and Plural Marriage: Church History Topics Ask a Question What Is the Book of Mormon? Explore Church History Where would you like to go next? Follow the historical record Compare accounts and source types in the wider Church History section. Read the book central to his prophetic claim Examine its teachings while distinguishing textual, historical, and spiritual questions. Continue the four-question study Carry your notes into another study: what the scriptures and records teach, what is becoming clearer, and what still needs attention. Use the reviewed videos and reflection questions to identify a useful next source. Then explore the restored Church study for the beliefs, ordinances, and community connected with this history. Read the source accounts Watch and study

records.title: Begin in the grove, then open the records
records.text: Watch and study Begin in the grove, then open the records The film Joseph Smith: The Prophet of the Restoration offers a dramatic introduction to his life and legacy. Begin your examination with his reported First Vision. Watch with a source question in mind: what can you identify in the written accounts, and what belongs to a filmmaker's portrayal? Church video Joseph Smith: The Prophet of the Restoration The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The Church's First Vision Accounts essay identifies four firsthand accounts. Its discussion of the 1832 account emphasizes Joseph's concern for forgiveness and personal redemption. The 1838 account places the vision within the beginnings of the Church and emphasizes his question about which church to join. These are different dates of recording, not four dates for the event. Begin with one account, noting its audience and emphasis. Then compare a second. The essay presents the Church's explanation of differences and links to documents so that you can examine more than a modern summary.

records.title: A Worked Example: Studying the First Vision
records.text: Read the account before the summary Joseph Smith History 1:5-20 recounts religious disagreement, Joseph's reading and prayer, and his reported vision. Record the questions he describes and the response he says he received. This is the scriptural account accepted by Latter-day Saints; identifying it as an account is important when studying history. Explore and study Joseph Smith's account in his own words A reader leans over Joseph Smith's written account with another book open beside it. Beginning with his own words lets the record speak before we decide what his life and testimony mean. Read Joseph Smith–History 1 Compare accounts with attention to when they were recorded Use the First Vision Accounts essay linked above to reach the other records. Compare emphasis, wording, audience, and date of recording. The date an event is said to have occurred and the date a surviving account was written are different facts. The essay offers the Church's interpretation of differences; the underlying documents allow you to examine the evidence yourself. Keep historical and spiritual questions distinct A historical investigation can ask what records survive and how they relate. A spiritual inquiry may ask what the Restoration claim means for belief and practice. Those inquiries can inform each other, but one should not silently stand in for the other. If a concern remains, name it specifically and pursue the relevant evidence. A useful source note Write the title, author or recorder, date of the record, and exact passage you are considering. Add a separate sentence for your interpretation. This keeps a later retelling from becoming indistinguishable from the original evidence.

records.title: From a personal inquiry to shared work
records.text: Watch and study From a personal inquiry to shared work Explore and study Joseph Smith's accounts across time A handwritten record lies open beside an inkwell on a nineteenth-century desk. Preserved across time, Joseph Smith's accounts let readers follow how he described his search for God in his own words. Joseph Smith History 1:5-20 Explore and study Oliver Cowdery joins the work Two readers place the revelation beside their notes, tracing the shared labor, uncertainty and reassurance surrounding Oliver Cowdery's work with Joseph Smith. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 In his October 2014 address Joseph Smith , Elder Neil L. Andersen discusses the Restoration and invites a personal witness through prayer and scripture. Compare his statement of faith with a revelation from the work surrounding the Book of Mormon. Read the heading to Doctrine and Covenants 6 as historical context. It identifies Harmony, Pennsylvania, April 1829, and Oliver Cowdery's work as a scribe beginning April 7. Church video Joseph Smith The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Verses 18-20 combine support with accountability. Oliver is asked to stand by Joseph in difficulty, and the two are to give and receive correction. Patience, faith, hope, and charity belong within that relationship. This is a useful passage to keep beside a history of religious leadership because the text itself makes room for faults and growth. In verses 21-23 the speaker identifies Himself as Jesus Christ and recalls peace given to Oliver. In verses 36-37 attention turns again to Christ and His wounds. Consider how the revelation directs a participant in the Restoration toward the Savior. Continue that connection in the full D&C 6:36 study .

records.title: A study you can carry into the week
records.text: These focusChrist prompts are invitations for personal reflection. Explore and study Bring the question to God A man bows his head beside a closed book on a quiet park bench, giving prayer and careful study room to work together as he seeks understanding. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 First session: establish the question Choose a single question about Joseph's life. Write it in language that a source could help answer: what did he report, when was it recorded, or how did a particular teaching develop? Avoid making one question stand for his entire life. Second session: follow a citation Open a document linked from the First Vision essay. Read the surrounding passage. Note the recorder, recording date, and what the document actually says. If your question concerns a different period, use the Church History section to find the relevant sources. Third session: assess the interpretation Write a short account of what you learned, separating evidence from your explanation of it. Name any remaining uncertainty. A source can establish what a witness reported without resolving every question about the experience being described. Fourth session: consider the spiritual claim Read D&C 6 with the historical questions still clearly named. What does its invitation to seek wisdom, accept correction, and look to Christ mean for your own conduct? Personal reflection can accompany careful investigation without replacing it. Bring a passage and a specific question to Ask , then check the response against the linked original sources.

records.title: Why Are Families Important in Latter-day Saint Belief?
records.pageTitle: Why Are Families Important in Latter-day Saint Belief?
records.text: Answers / Families Latter-day Saints believe family is central to God’s plan because every person is a child of heavenly parents and because family relationships can become eternal through Jesus Christ and sacred covenants. Watch and study How Does Eternal Hope Shape a Home? Explore and study Practice patient companionship A father patiently helps his daughter tie her shoe. Small moments of gentleness can express the long-suffering and love that should guide family relationships. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121 In Eternal Families , President Henry B. Eyring connects the hope of family life with God to everyday service. Speaking to priesthood holders, he asks them to place their families and the families around them at the center of their concern. Near the end, he emphasizes the lasting value of small acts that help loved ones move toward eternal life. General conference video and text Eternal Families The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2016 Watch or read with two questions in mind: What does he teach about covenants? How does he describe the way family members should treat one another? He draws on Doctrine and Covenants 121:41-43 , emphasizing persuasion, patience, gentleness, and sincere love. As a personal application, consider a small act of care that fits your circumstances: listening without interruption, offering an apology for your own mistake, or keeping a promise. Eternal family teaching can give those ordinary choices meaning. It does not let us determine the worth or ultimate future of someone else's household. People come to this question from many circumstances: marriage, singleness, parenting, adoption, or life in a blended family. Some also carry grief, infertility, divorce, or painful relationships. Those experiences deserve individual care, without assumptions about anyone's faith or worth. We Belong to the Family of God Latter-day Saint teaching begins with divine identity: human beings lived with heavenly parents before birth and are sons and daughters of God. Earthly family life is therefore connected to a larger eternal family and provides a setting for learning love, sacrifice, responsibility, forgiveness, and service. Marriage and Parenting Matter Church teaching gives high importance to marriage, parenting, fidelity, nurturing children, and building homes centered on Jesus Christ. The family is viewed not merely as a social convenience but as part of God’s design for mortal growth and eternal happiness. What Does It Mean for a Family to Be Eternal? Latter-day Saints believe priesthood sealing ordinances performed in temples can unite husbands and wives, and parents and children, beyond death. These promises are connected to faithfulness to God and the covenants made in the temple. The doctrine is one reason temples and family history hold such a prominent place in Church life. What About Imperfect or Painful Family Situations? No family is perfect, and some relationships are unsafe or deeply wounded. The gospel does not require a person to pretend that abuse or serious harm is acceptable. The hope of eternal family life is centered on Jesus Christ’s power to redeem, heal, judge perfectly, and make right what cannot be fully repaired in mortality. Why This Belief Affects Everyday Life If relationships can matter eternally, daily choices toward patience, loyalty, repentance, forgiveness, teaching, and service gain added significance. Latter-day Saints are encouraged to strengthen family relationships while also extending Christlike love to people in every family circumstance. When Family Teachings Touch a Tender Place If talk of eternal families brings up longing or unanswered questions, you are welcome to take your time. You do not owe anyone a public explanation of your family life. For more focused reading, see support through divorce or hope after the death of a child . Care That Reaches Beyond One Household Family study can lead to a practical question: who needs care around me today? Mosiah 18:8-10 asks disciples to share burdens and offer comfort. That commitment can include a neighbor living alone, a parent needing a break, or someone whose relatives are far away. You might offer an invitation with room to decline, ask how someone prefers to be included, or help with an ordinary task. Belonging is easier to experience when people are known by name and treated with consideration, without having to explain why their household looks different. Study Belonging Alongside Responsibility Explore and study Let care extend beyond your household A parent and teenager clear an older neighbor's path together. Their care extends family discipleship outward through service that respects what the neighbor needs. Mosiah 18:8-9 Begin with people who need to be received Mark 10:13-16 shows adults bringing children to Jesus and disciples trying to turn them away. Jesus corrects that response and welcomes the children. Consider how a family or congregation could make room for a child who is shy, restless, disabled, or unfamiliar with worship. These are possible applications of welcome, not details supplied by the account. Explore and study Belonging means caring for one another Siblings work through a household task together, listening as they go. The ordinary moment carries the vision in Romans 12 of belonging to one body and caring for one another with affection. Read Romans 12 Love includes concrete care Romans 12:9-18 speaks of sincere love, hospitality, shared joy and sorrow, and seeking peace as far as it lies within one's power. The qualification matters: one person cannot control every relationship. Reflect on what care is yours to offer and where you need support or appropriate boundaries. Faithfulness and imperfect circumstances A teaching about the purpose of family is not a complete explanation of any particular household. Avoid turning an ideal into a ranking of people's worth. When family language brings grief or exclusion, it may help to talk with someone who can listen without requiring a defense of your circumstances. One practical way to use this study Choose one person and one form of care you can offer reliably. Ask what would help rather than assuming. If the subject raises more pain than clarity today, pause with the children's artwork study or use the focused resources on loss and divorce. Watch and study See Each Child as Someone to Know Explore and study Let someone be heard A mother listens while her teenage son speaks on the front steps. Gentleness and honest attention can keep love present in a difficult family conversation. Read Ephesians 4 Explore and study Make space for each person’s voice A multigenerational family listens as a teenager shares from their reading. Around the table, every age and question is welcomed, and kindness in Christ keeps the family learning together. Ephesians 4:31-32 3 Nephi 17:11-24 describes the Savior praying among the people and blessing their children individually. Read the account alongside the teaching about attentive parenting below. The multitude makes room for the children to come near Him, and their care receives the attention of the whole gathering. General conference video and text Fathers The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2016 In Fathers , Elder D. Todd Christofferson affirms equal partnership between parents, honors single fathers, foster fathers, and stepfathers, and recognizes circumstances requiring support and adaptation. He explicitly rejects abuse in discipline. For a parent, relative, teacher, or friend, these teachings can prompt a question about attention: what do I know about this child's interests, worries, and hopes? Listening to a child and following through on a promise are ordinary ways to practice care. You do not need to compare your household with another family's circumstances to choose a loving action today. A conversation about belonging If this would be useful, discuss one question with a willing family member or trusted friend: When have you felt heard here? What helps you feel included? Is there something we could do differently? Receive the answer without requiring agreement about every issue. Where there has been harm, a safe setting and qualified support may be needed before a joint conversation is appropriate. Official Sources and Further Study Family: Gospel Study Guide The Family: A Proclamation to the World About Temple Sealings Ask a Question Why Temples? What Happens After Death? Where would you like to go next? Study eternal marriage in depth Explore sealing, covenant faithfulness, equal partnership, tender questions, and a seven-day scripture path centered on Christ. Study Christ’s welcome of children Read two scriptural scenes and reflect on concrete ways to make room for children. When family life includes divorce Explore faith, dignity, boundaries, and support without an idealized family story.

records.title: Why Do Latter-day Saints Build Temples?
records.pageTitle: Why Do Latter-day Saints Build Temples?
records.keywords: why latter day saints build temples
records.text: Answers / Temples Latter-day Saints build temples because they believe God has commanded His people to create sacred places where worshippers make covenants, receive ordinances, learn of Jesus Christ, and seek blessings that extend beyond death. Temples are not the same as ordinary Sunday meetinghouses. This page summarizes Latter-day Saint belief; official Church temple resources are linked below. Watch and study See the purpose behind the building Explore and study Begin with the purpose of worship Two friends read scripture together on a shaded garden terrace. Their quiet study turns toward the Kirtland dedicatory prayer and its longing for learning, holiness and God's help. Read Doctrine and Covenants 109 Begin with Temples Through Time , which brings together scholars and people of different faiths to discuss ancient and modern temples. Listen for both shared interests and the distinct Latter-day Saint understanding explained on this page. The significance of a temple is best understood through what worshippers believe happens there. Church video Temples Through Time The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Doctrine and Covenants 109:1-15 records the Kirtland Temple dedication prayer in March 1836. The prayer asks the Father to accept the house in the name of Jesus Christ and seeks learning, holiness, and His presence. Study and faith appear together in verses 7 and 14 . Continue through verses 21-23 . The prayer includes repentance and restoration to blessings, then asks that servants leave the temple strengthened to share the gospel. This provides a pattern to consider: worship prepares people to go outward in service. It does not make the building an escape from the responsibilities of daily life. A House of the Lord A dedicated temple is regarded as a holy house of the Lord. Latter-day Saints connect modern temples with a scriptural pattern of sacred places where God teaches, covenants with, and blesses His people. Covenants and Ordinances A covenant is a sacred commitment between a person and God. An ordinance is a sacred religious act performed by priesthood authority. The Church explains these terms in Why Ordinances and Covenants Matter . Temple worship includes ordinances that are not performed in ordinary chapels. The endowment teaches God’s plan and includes covenants to follow Jesus Christ. Temple sealings unite husbands and wives and connect children to parents with the promise that family relationships can continue eternally when covenants are faithfully kept. Jesus Christ Is Central to Temple Worship Temple worship is intended to point disciples toward the Savior. The ordinances teach about God’s plan of salvation, the Atonement of Jesus Christ, obedience, sacrifice, consecrated discipleship, and the hope of returning to God through Christ. Why Are Some Temple Ceremonies Limited to Prepared Members? Before dedication, temples often hold public open houses. After dedication, participation in temple ordinances is reserved for Church members who have prepared spiritually and are recommended by local Church leaders. Latter-day Saints describe this as sacred preparation rather than secrecy: the covenants are treated as solemn commitments requiring readiness. What About People Who Have Died? Latter-day Saints believe God provides every person a fair opportunity to receive the gospel. In temples, living members may receive ordinances by proxy for deceased ancestors. Those ordinances are understood as an offer, not a forced conversion; the deceased retain agency to accept or reject them. When Temple Questions Are Personal For some readers, temple teachings bring hope; for others, they bring questions about a loved one, divorce, or circumstances that did not turn out as expected. A short explanation of sealing cannot resolve every individual situation. The official temple sealing overview explains the teaching, while a trusted Church leader can help with questions about your own participation. If the subject is tender, you may prefer to begin with families and belonging or support through divorce . There is no need to share private family details here in order to keep learning. Understand the Connections Behind Temple Worship Explore and study Prepare through learning Open scriptures, a notebook and a folded jacket wait in readiness for worship. The Kirtland dedicatory prayer teaches that preparation for God's house includes learning, faith and order. Doctrine and Covenants 109:7-8 Covenants grow from a relationship with God Mosiah 18:8-10 describes baptismal commitment in terms of bearing burdens, offering comfort, and serving God. These are baptismal teachings, not a description of the temple ceremony. They provide a familiar starting point for understanding why a covenant is meant to shape ordinary conduct as well as worship. Why do Latter-day Saints speak of restored keys? Doctrine and Covenants 110:1-10, 13-16 records a vision in the Kirtland Temple and the appearance of Elijah. Latter-day Saints connect this account with restored authority for temple work. Here keys means authority to direct particular priesthood work, not a physical object. The passage belongs to the Church's Restoration account and should be read in that setting. Service reaches beyond the living Read Doctrine and Covenants 138:30-35, 58-59 to connect temple service with teaching among the dead. Proxy describes one person performing an ordinance on behalf of another. It does not mean someone else's faith or willingness is decided for them. Keep the official temple resources beside this study when exploring the Church's explanation. How could this affect life outside the temple? Reflect on whether a promise to follow Christ is changing how you treat someone today. Service, honesty, and care for family and neighbors give a practical setting for considering covenant discipleship. No visitor needs to disclose their membership or temple status to use this study. Watch and study Covenant worship and joy in Christ Explore and study Connect worship with daily commitments A father and adult daughter talk while sharing the work of washing and drying dishes, connecting promises to God with patient care in daily life. Mosiah 18:8-10 Explore and study Temple building across generations Craftsmen measure and shape heavy stone with patience. Piece by piece, their devoted labor prepares a house where generations will come to worship God. Return to the Kirtland dedicatory prayer The Church's public overview of the endowment explains how temple instruction relates the Creation, Fall, and Atonement to God's plan. It also describes covenants involving obedience, sacrifice, gospel living, chastity, and consecration. Read those explanations directly so that the terms have more meaning than a list. Church video The Temple and Your Spiritual Foundation The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The same overview encourages participants to learn over time and says they need not understand everything on their first visit. Preparation includes learning what one is committing to and choosing that commitment prayerfully. A quiet or unfamiliar experience does not need to be compared with someone else's description. In the accompanying October 2021 message, The Temple and Your Spiritual Foundation , President Russell M. Nelson connects temple covenants with a foundation in Jesus Christ. His complete address also discusses learning through continuing revelation. As a personal reflection, ask how temple learning might deepen gratitude for Him. Joy can be expressed through patient service, keeping a promise, or extending care to a family member. These are practical invitations, not a measure of another person's spiritual worth. A study you can carry into the week These focusChrist prompts are invitations for personal reflection. Explore and study Carry a covenant into daily care Two neighbors clear fallen branches from an older neighbor's path. The work is practical and personal, quietly fulfilling the baptismal promise to help carry another's burden. Read Mosiah 18:8–10 Understand a word Choose covenant, ordinance, endowment, or sealing. Read its explanation in the official resources and put it into your own words. Ask what the teaching says about the relationship between God and the person making the commitment. Connect worship and conduct Choose one ordinary responsibility that could receive greater care: your use of time, honesty at work, attention to family, or service to a neighbor. Consider what covenant discipleship would look like in that specific setting this week. Prepare an honest question If you are preparing to attend, bring questions about preparation and participation to your bishop or branch president. If you are simply learning, use the public introduction and source pages freely. This study does not require you to disclose your membership or personal circumstances. Remember an individual Consider learning one accurate detail about an ancestor or preserving a family memory with permission. Let your interest begin with a person's life and relationships. The section on service for the dead explains the belief behind proxy ordinances and the importance of agency. Bring a passage and a specific question to Ask , then check the response against the linked original sources. Official Sources and Further Study Why Latter-day Saints Build Temples Temples: Topics and Questions About Temple Sealings Ask a Question Why Families Matter Where would you like to go next? Read about life after death Understand the beliefs behind temple service for those who have died. Explore family relationships and belonging Consider eternal hopes alongside the varied realities of family life now. Watch an introduction to temple worship Hear an official explanation of temples, then continue with resources about listening and belonging at home.

Church video The Temple and Your Spiritual Foundation The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The same overview encourages participants to learn over time and says they need not understand everything on their first visit. Preparation includes learning what one is committing to and choosing that commitment prayerfully. A quiet or unfamiliar experience does not need to be compared with someone else's description. In the accompanying October 2021 message, The Temple and Your Spiritual Foundation , President Russell M. Nelson connects temple covenants with a foundation in Jesus Christ. His complete address also discusses learning through continuing revelation. As a personal reflection, ask how temple learning might deepen gratitude for Him. Joy can be expressed through patient service, keeping a promise, or extending care to a family member. These are practical invitations, not a measure of another person's spiritual worth.

records.title: Be Still - Art & Study
records.text: Inspirational Art / Be Still Christ walks shoulder to shoulder with a burdened man while the city rushes around them. “Be still” becomes more than escape from noise. It becomes the courage to recognize who walks beside us. A path through this study Find Christ in the Press of the Day The man in the artwork has not stepped outside modern life. Cars, buildings, and other people remain close. Yet Christ is closer. Begin there, then read Psalm 46 in its full setting of shaking earth, roaring water, and unsettled nations. Look Notice the burdened posture of the man and the Savior's steady place beside him. Read Hear “be still” inside a psalm about refuge, upheaval, and God's presence. Respond Choose one faithful action for today and one outcome you can entrust to God. Scripture study Stillness in the Middle of Upheaval Psalm 46 opens with God as refuge and strength. The earth moves, waters roar, and kingdoms shake. The invitation to be still comes near the end, after the psalmist has described God bringing conflict to an end. Biblical stillness is not denial. It is a reorientation toward the God who remains present when the world feels unstable. The Lord repeats the invitation in Doctrine and Covenants 101:13-17 . Here too, comfort comes to people living through distress. The command and promise belong together: be still, and know that He is God. Peace with the storm still close In Mark 4:35-41 , frightened disciples wake Jesus in a storm. He calms the sea and then asks about their fear and faith. John 14:27 adds a promise of peace that differs from what the world gives. Together, the passages invite us to seek Christ's presence without pretending every storm ends on our preferred schedule. Look again Peace That Walks with Us These artworks do not all show quiet surroundings. They show companionship, trust, and release within real movement and strain. The Savior in the Storm Wind and water fill the boat, but the disciples are not alone. Read the fear, their cry for help, and the great calm in Mark 4:35-41 . Closer Than the Noise Traffic and crowds continue around them, yet Christ matches the man's pace and listens. His promise of peace meets life as it is in John 14:27 . A Breath Before the Next Step No answer is being forced in this moment. The still water and closed journal allow time to remember the refuge named in Psalm 46 . Peace with Work Still to Do The burden is not imagined away; it is lifted together. Faithful stillness can lead into willing action, as taught in Doctrine and Covenants 58:26-28 . Quiet reflection Be Still, Then Walk Forward Stillness can prepare the heart for faithful action. Open one prompt and stay with it for a few minutes. What remains steady when life feels unsettled? Read Psalm 46 and list what changes in the chapter. Then list what the psalm says about God. Let the contrast shape a short, honest prayer. What can I do, and what can I entrust to God? Name one responsibility you can act on today. Then name one outcome you cannot control. Doctrine and Covenants 58:26-28 can help you hold agency and trust together. Who could use a quiet companion? The Savior in the artwork does not speak from across the street. Think of someone whose burden may need your presence more than your advice. Anchor Stillness in Jesus Christ In “Be Still, and Know That I Am God” , Elder David A. Bednar connects spiritual stillness with covenant confidence in Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ. Read it beside Psalm 46 rather than treating stillness as a technique by itself. records.title: Suffer the Little Children - Art & Study
records.pageTitle: Suffer the Little Children - Art & Study
records.text: Inspirational Art / Suffer the Little Children Children press close to Jesus without fear. One rests against Him, another reaches toward Him, and the Savior receives their trust with complete attention. A path through this study Come Close Without Fear The painting is full of touch, movement, and trust. Jesus is not speaking to a distant crowd; He is giving the children His time. The Gospel accounts make that welcome even more striking because the disciples had tried to turn them away. Look Notice each child's posture and the calm attention Jesus gives them. Read Follow the movement from being rebuked at the edge to being held and blessed. Respond Ask what helps a child or vulnerable person feel safe, heard, and cherished. Scripture study He Took Them in His Arms Read Mark 10:13-16 slowly. People bring children to Jesus so He can touch them. The disciples object, but Jesus is displeased with the barrier they create. He calls the children to Him, takes them in His arms, places His hands upon them, and blesses them. His welcome is spoken and embodied. Jesus also teaches the adults: the kingdom of God must be received as a little child. The passage honors qualities such as trust and openness without pretending children never feel fear or pain. The adults around them carry a sacred responsibility to protect, listen, and lead with love. A day of prayer, tears, and joy at Bountiful In 3 Nephi 17 , Jesus perceives that the people desire Him to remain. He heals their sick, prays with them, and asks that their little children be brought to Him. The chapter lingers over compassion. Read verses 21-24 and notice what the children receive and what the gathered adults are allowed to witness. Look again Every Child Drawn Near These artworks carry the same welcome into different places and relationships. Open each one at full size before reading the scripture beside it. Unhurried Welcome One child rests against Him while another shares a small treasure. Jesus gives them His full attention, just as He takes the children into His arms in Mark 10:13-16 . Gentleness at Her Pace Christ lowers Himself to the child's eye level and waits with an open hand. The small distance between them makes His invitation, “forbid them not” in Mark 10:14 , feel especially tender. Joy in Every Place The children are not a background around Jesus; their voices and faces fill the circle. His invitation is extended “unto all” in 2 Nephi 26:33 . Time Enough to Listen The child holds a stone and a story; the Savior turns toward both. Matthew 18:1-5 asks adults to learn from a child rather than look past one. Quiet reflection Receive and Protect Use these questions for prayer, a journal, or a family conversation. What do I see in the children's faces and hands? Look again before answering. Notice who is reaching, resting, watching, or smiling. What does Jesus do that allows closeness and trust? How can I listen to a child more fully? Choose one ordinary moment this week to put distractions down, listen without interrupting, and take a child's words seriously. What does Christlike protection require? The Savior removed a barrier and welcomed the children. Consider whether a family, congregation, school, or community practice needs more patience, safety, or attentive care from you. Keep the Children at the Center For a child-friendly retelling, read Jesus Blesses the Little Children . For further teaching about our responsibility toward children, continue with Little Children by President Boyd K. Packer. records.title: The Good Shepherd - Art & Study
records.text: Inspirational Art / The Good Shepherd The Savior moves through a crowded street with a warm, attentive expression. The image carries the tenderness of a Shepherd who knows His sheep, seeks the wandering, and never treats a wounded life as an inconvenience. A path through this study Listen for the Shepherd's Voice Look first at the Savior's face and the life moving around Him. He is not distant from the street or the people in it. John 10 gives language to that closeness: He knows, calls, leads, protects, and lays down His life for the sheep. Look Notice the Savior's expression and the people nearest Him in the crowded street. Read Listen for every action Jesus uses to describe the Good Shepherd in John 10 . Respond Consider one person you can notice, call, or walk beside with greater care. Scripture study Known, Led, and Loved In John 10:1-18 , Jesus describes a relationship built on recognition and trust. The shepherd knows the sheep and calls them; the sheep recognize his voice and follow. The image grows deeper when Jesus says the Good Shepherd gives His life for the sheep. His care is not sentimental. It is costly, faithful, and personal. Psalm 23 adds the language of provision, rest, guidance, and companionship through the valley of the shadow of death. The shepherd does not promise a path with no valley. He promises His presence through it. The sheep beyond the present fold Jesus speaks of “other sheep” in John 10:16 . In 3 Nephi 15:11-24 , the risen Christ identifies the people at Bountiful with that promise. Read the two passages together and notice how His voice reaches people in more than one place. Look again The Shepherd Draws Near These scenes place the Savior beside people in need of healing, strength, and companionship. Open each artwork, then let the linked passage shape what you see. Gathered into His Arms The lamb rests against the Shepherd while the flock follows through rough country. Isaiah's promise is both strong and tender in Isaiah 40:11 . The One Is Not Overlooked The street keeps moving, but Jesus stops and comes close. His parable in Luke 15:3-7 counts one wandering sheep as worth seeking. Strength Shared Under Strain Mud and effort cover everyone in the scene. The Savior's focused care gives weight to His invitation for the weary in Matthew 11:28-30 . Known in a Crowd Many faces fill the street, yet Jesus looks toward one man and calls him down by name. Follow the welcome and change in Luke 19:1-10 . Quiet reflection Hear and Follow Choose the prompt that feels most honest today. Where have I noticed the Shepherd's care? Read Psalm 23 slowly. Name one place where you have received rest, direction, nourishment, or companionship. Offer thanks for the person or moment through which that care came. Which voice am I learning to trust? John 10 describes sheep recognizing the shepherd's voice. Compare a thought that leads toward Christlike love with one that produces contempt or despair. What fruit does each voice bear? Who might need someone to walk beside them? Think of one person who may feel unseen or burdened. Choose a small act of steady care: listen, send a message, share a meal, or help with something practical. Study the Shepherd's Compassion In Our Good Shepherd , Elder Dale G. Renlund teaches about the Savior's compassion for imperfect people and His joy as they heal. You can also follow the theme through the Good Shepherd entry in the Guide to the Scriptures . records.title: The Living Christ - Art & Study
records.text: Inspirational Art / The Living Christ The portrait meets us with light, warmth, and an open expression. Christian hope rests on the witness that Jesus Christ rose from the tomb and still calls people by name. A path through this study Come Near to the Living Christ Begin with the face in the portrait. The light is bright, yet the Savior's expression is gentle. Nothing in the image asks us to hurry past Him. Let that first impression accompany you into the Resurrection accounts, where grief, fear, recognition, and joy all unfold in the presence of the risen Lord. Look Notice the light, the Savior's expression, and where your attention settles first. Read Walk through John 20 with Mary Magdalene, the gathered disciples, and Thomas. Respond Name one way belief in a living Savior changes the way you meet this day. Scripture study Follow the Witnesses in John 20 John 20:1-18 begins before the morning is clear. Mary comes to the tomb carrying grief and discovers that the stone has been moved. She does not recognize Jesus until He speaks her name. The change in the account is deeply personal: sorrow becomes recognition, and recognition becomes a message she is trusted to carry. Continue with John 20:19-31 . The disciples are behind closed doors when Jesus comes among them and speaks peace. Thomas receives time, an invitation to see, and a reason to believe. John closes by telling readers why these signs were written: that they might believe Jesus is the Christ and find life in His name. Why the Resurrection reaches beyond one morning Paul connects Christ's Resurrection with the promised resurrection of humankind in 1 Corinthians 15:12-22 . The hope is not that death is insignificant. The hope is that death will not have the final word. That promise can be precious even when grief is still present. Look again Four Images of His Continuing Care Each image turns toward a different human need. Open any artwork to explore its scripture and study options, view the full-size picture, or continue the lesson. Called by Name Morning light reaches the garden as Mary turns toward the voice she knows. Stay with the tenderness of recognition in John 20:11-18 . Peace Behind Closed Doors Fear has gathered the disciples into one room. Christ comes among them with open hands and the first gift He names is peace in John 20:19-23 . Faith Met with Patience Jesus does not reduce Thomas to a label. He meets him face to face and answers his longing to know. Read the encounter in John 20:24-29 . Hope That Does Not Rush Grief The open Bible and quiet companionship hold sorrow and hope in the same morning. The risen Christ's promise reaches toward mourning in John 11:25-26 . Quiet reflection Let the Witness Become Personal These prompts are invitations, not a test. Open the one that meets you today. When have I felt known by name? Return to Mary in John 20:11-18 . Sit for a moment with the change that comes when Jesus speaks her name. Write the name of someone who may need to feel remembered today. What closed door am I standing behind? The disciples received the words “Peace be unto you” while the doors were shut. Name one fear you can bring honestly to Christ, without pretending it has already disappeared. What does the Living Christ invite me to do next? Read one paragraph of The Living Christ . Choose one truth about the Savior to carry into prayer, worship, or service this week. Read the Witness in Full The Living Christ: The Testimony of the Apostles gathers apostolic testimony of the Savior's life, Atonement, Resurrection, present ministry, and promised return. For a second voice, study The Resurrection of Jesus Christ by Elder D. Todd Christofferson. records.title: Come Near to the Living Christ
records.text: Begin with the face in the portrait. The light is bright, yet the Savior's expression is gentle. Nothing in the image asks us to hurry past Him. Let that first impression accompany you into the Resurrection accounts, where grief, fear, recognition, and joy all unfold in the presence of the risen Lord. Look Notice the light, the Savior's expression, and where your attention settles first. Read Walk through John 20 with Mary Magdalene, the gathered disciples, and Thomas. Respond Name one way belief in a living Savior changes the way you meet this day.

records.title: Follow the Witnesses in John 20
records.text: Scripture study Follow the Witnesses in John 20 John 20:1-18 begins before the morning is clear. Mary comes to the tomb carrying grief and discovers that the stone has been moved. She does not recognize Jesus until He speaks her name. The change in the account is deeply personal: sorrow becomes recognition, and recognition becomes a message she is trusted to carry. Continue with John 20:19-31 . The disciples are behind closed doors when Jesus comes among them and speaks peace. Thomas receives time, an invitation to see, and a reason to believe. John closes by telling readers why these signs were written: that they might believe Jesus is the Christ and find life in His name. Why the Resurrection reaches beyond one morning Paul connects Christ's Resurrection with the promised resurrection of humankind in 1 Corinthians 15:12-22 . The hope is not that death is insignificant. The hope is that death will not have the final word. That promise can be precious even when grief is still present.

records.title: Let the Witness Become Personal

What closed door am I standing behind? The disciples received the words “Peace be unto you” while the doors were shut. Name one fear you can bring honestly to Christ, without pretending it has already disappeared. What does the Living Christ invite me to do next? Read one paragraph of The Living Christ . For example, read John 20:24-31 and notice Thomas's absence, his later encounter with Jesus, and the author's explanation for writing. You might ask, “How does this account speak to readers who were not there?” That question is more specific than asking for a general statement about doubt. Read the response alongside the source. Check whether it explains the passage's setting, distinguishes the text from an application, and leaves room for what the passage does not settle. A fluent answer still needs checking. You can ask a follow-up about a verse or an unfamiliar term, and you are free to disagree with an interpretation. Continue the John 20 study Walk through Mary, the disciples, and Thomas; then consider why resurrection matters. When your question is personal Explore scripture and discernment without treating an automated response as personal revelation. When two passages seem different Use a comparison that preserves context and separates the text from your own conclusions. You do not have to share private experiences to study here. A general question can be enough. For a structured way to keep Christ central while working through difficult questions, continue to the Stand Forever study . records.title: The Atonement of Jesus Christ
records.text: An invitation to linger Because He lives, we can begin again Jesus Christ is at the heart of this study. His suffering in Gethsemane and on the cross, His death, and His Resurrection open the way home to our Heavenly Father. We come to Him with sins to forsake, sorrows to share, questions to ask, and hope that may still be small. He invites us to come. Begin with John 3:16–17 and the official Atonement of Jesus Christ study guide . Follow the story from the beginning, or choose the part you need today. Open any picture for its scripture and study options. The artwork offers reverent, imaginative scenes; the linked scriptures provide the accounts we study. 01 · Before the world Before the world: chosen from the beginning The Beloved Son and the Father's will The Pearl of Great Price takes the story of redemption back before mortal life. Moses records the Beloved Son's willingness to do the Father's will and give Him the glory. Abraham describes the council before the world and the choice of one who would be sent. Jesus Christ's mission belongs within the Father's loving purpose for His children. Moses 4:1–4 · Abraham 3:22–28 · Moses 1:39 Explore the picture and scripture The heavens above us Stars fill the sky above still water. Let the quiet of this imagined landscape lead you to the scriptures about Jesus Christ, the Creator. Moses 2:1 John 1:1–5 Pause and reflect Read the Son's response in Moses 4:2 beside His prayer in Luke 22:42. What continuity do you see in His willingness to serve the Father? Creation belongs to the story Moses records God creating through His Only Begotten. John's Gospel identifies the Word who was with God and through whom all things were made. The Savior who came into mortality is also the Creator. His love for the world is personal. Moses 2:1 · John 1:1–5, 14 · Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 Official Church study guide Atonement of Jesus Christ Begin with the Church’s guide, then follow its questions and scriptures into a deeper personal study. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Continue · Why a Savior? ↓ All chapters ↑ 02 · Why a Savior? Why we need a Savior Mortal life, agency, and the Fall Our lives include real choices and real consequences. Lehi places agency within God's plan and teaches that redemption comes through the Holy Messiah. The Fall brought mortality and separation from God's presence; Jesus Christ makes redemption possible. We are also responsible for our own sins. Our need for Him includes both the death we cannot prevent and the sins from which we cannot cleanse ourselves. Explore the picture and scripture The road through mortality A path leads from green shelter into open, rugged country. Read Lehi’s teaching about agency and redemption. 2 Nephi 2 Read 2 Nephi 2:6–9, 22–27 and Mosiah 3:17 . Justice and mercy Alma does not treat wrongdoing as unimportant. He teaches that mercy reaches the repentant through the Redeemer while justice remains real. Repentance is possible because of Christ. His invitation gives us a reason to face the truth about our choices and a way to move forward. Read Alma 42:13–25 . Reflect: What changes when I see repentance as an invitation from someone who loves me? Deeper reading: 2 Nephi 9 , Alma 34:8–17 , Moses 5:9–12 . Explore the picture and scripture The Shepherd seeks the one The sheep rests in His arms. Jesus tells of a shepherd who goes after the one that is lost. Luke 15:3–7 Continue · The promise ↓ All chapters ↑ 03 · The promise The promise reaches Adam, Eve, and the prophets Redemption taught from the beginning An angel taught Adam that sacrifice pointed to the Only Begotten. Adam and Eve heard the promise of redemption and rejoiced. Enoch's teaching connects the Fall, repentance, baptism, the Spirit, and the blood of the Only Begotten. The invitation to come to Christ runs through these earliest accounts. Moses 5:5–12 · Moses 6:48–62 Explore the picture and scripture Hope beyond Eden Two figures face the morning beside cultivated ground and a simple altar. This imagined scene of Adam and Eve invites us to read the promise of redemption they received. Moses 5:5–12 Enoch sees the Redeemer Enoch mourned as he saw human wickedness and suffering. He also saw the coming of the Son of Man, the cross, and the promise of resurrection. The vision joins sorrow with hope. Read the account carefully and notice where Enoch's attention turns toward the Savior. Moses 7:44–47, 53–57 · Moses 7:62 The Lamb and the suffering servant The Passover account tells of deliverance. Isaiah speaks of the servant who bears grief and sorrow. John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God. Read these passages together and consider how scripture prepares us to understand His sacrifice. Exodus 12:1–14 · Isaiah 53:3–7 · John 1:29 · 1 Corinthians 5:7 Pause and reflect Which image helps you understand Him today: Creator, Redeemer, Lamb, Shepherd, or the One who carries our sorrows? Follow one title through its linked passages. Explore the picture and scripture Remembering deliverance Bread, herbs, a cup, and a lamp invite a pause to remember Passover. This symbolic still life leads to the account of deliverance and to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God. Exodus 12:1–14 John 1:29 Continue · His sacrifice ↓ All chapters ↑ 04 · His sacrifice His willing sacrifice At the table Before Gethsemane, Jesus shared bread and the cup with His Apostles. Remembering Him would become part of their worship. Read slowly and notice how personally He speaks about His body and blood. Luke 22:14–20 · Matthew 26:26–29 Explore the picture and scripture In remembrance of Him Bread and a cup rest on a quiet table. Return to the Savior’s words at the Last Supper. Luke 22:14–20 In Gethsemane Jesus prayed to the Father in anguish and submitted to His will. The account calls for reverence. We can attend to His words without pretending to measure everything He endured. In latter-day revelation, the Savior speaks of His suffering and invites us to repent. Luke 22:39–46 · Doctrine and Covenants 19:16–19 Explore the picture and scripture Not my will, but thine Under the olive trees, Jesus bows in prayer. Read His words to the Father. Luke 22:39–46 At the cross John records the title placed on the cross, the two others crucified beside Jesus, and His mother standing nearby. Even there, He spoke to His mother and the beloved disciple about their care for one another. He later declared His work finished and died. His burial followed; His Resurrection would transform the disciples' grief. John 19:17–30 · Matthew 27:45–54 · John 19:38–42 Sensitive scene: The Crucifixion This artwork depicts the Savior’s suffering. You may continue reading without viewing it. Show image — At the cross Hide image — At the cross Explore the picture and scripture At the cross From above and behind the cross, we look toward the people gathered below and Jerusalem beyond. John records the Savior’s love and His finished work. John 19:17–30 Matthew 27:45–54 Pause and reflect What do His words reveal about His love? Read John 10:17–18 and 3 Nephi 27:13–16 . Sensitive scene: The Crucifixion This artwork depicts the Savior’s suffering. You may continue reading without viewing it. Show image — Those who stayed nearby Hide image — Those who stayed nearby Explore the picture and scripture Those who stayed nearby From beside and behind the cross, we see those who have stayed nearby. John records the Savior’s tender care for His mother and the beloved disciple. John 19:25–27 Conference message · Watch or read The Purifying Power of Gethsemane Bruce R. McConkie bears witness of the Savior’s sacrifice. Read or listen, then return to the Gospel accounts. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Conference message · Watch or read None Were with Him Jeffrey R. Holland follows the Savior’s lonely journey and bears witness of His love for us. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Conference message · Watch or read Lifted Up upon the Cross Jeffrey R. Holland reflects on the cross and the meaning of following Jesus Christ. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Continue · He is risen ↓ All chapters ↑ 05 · He is risen Resurrection and living hope The tomb was empty. Mary Magdalene encountered the risen Lord. The disciples' witness concerns a living Savior, not only the memory of a teacher they loved. John 20:1–18 · Luke 24:36–43 Explore the picture and scripture The tomb was empty Morning light enters a rock-cut tomb. Read the witnesses’ accounts of the risen Savior. John 20:1–9 Through Jesus Christ, everyone will be resurrected: spirit and body will be reunited. Eternal life with God is a distinct gift. Christ invites us to receive it through faith in Him, repentance, His ordinances and covenants, and faithful discipleship. 1 Corinthians 15:20–22 · Alma 11:42–45 · 3 Nephi 27:19–21 Explore the picture and scripture Mary A woman turns toward the risen Jesus in a garden. John records that He called Mary by name. John 20:11–18 Pause and reflect How does the promise of Resurrection change the way I remember someone I love? Explore the picture and scripture Along the road Jesus walks beside two listeners on a country road. Read how He opened the scriptures to the disciples traveling to Emmaus. Luke 24:13–32 Official Church study guide Resurrection Follow the scripture witnesses and explore the promise of life beyond death. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Continue · One by one ↓ All chapters ↑ 06 · One by one The Book of Mormon witnesses of His love A Redeemer promised Nephi's vision joins the birth and ministry of the Son of God with an explanation of God's love. King Benjamin teaches of the Savior's suffering and the salvation that comes through Him. Abinadi draws on Isaiah, and Alma speaks of the Redeemer's intimate knowledge of pain. These witnesses prepare readers to recognize Jesus Christ. 1 Nephi 11:13–33 · Mosiah 3:5–11 · Mosiah 14 · Alma 7:10–13 Explore the picture and scripture He had compassion on them Jesus leans toward an older woman as others wait nearby. Read of His compassion and healing among the people in the Book of Mormon. 3 Nephi 17:5–9 One by one The risen Jesus invited the people to come forward and know that He was the God of Israel who had been slain for the sins of the world. They came one by one. Later He healed their sick, prayed for them, and blessed their children. His ministry gives the doctrine a personal setting: people heard Him, approached Him, and received His compassion. 3 Nephi 11:10–17 · 3 Nephi 17:5–9, 11–24 · 3 Nephi 18:1–11 Pause and reflect What do you notice when you read the account slowly, one person at a time? Which invitation would you like to respond to today? An invitation that remains open Moroni ends with an invitation to come to Christ and be perfected in Him. The book's testimony leads to a relationship with the Savior and a life changed through His grace. Moroni 10:32–33 · 2 Nephi 26:23–28, 33 Continue · His living voice ↓ All chapters ↑ 07 · His living voice His living voice in the Doctrine and Covenants Hear the Savior speak In modern revelation Jesus Christ speaks of His suffering, calls us to repent, and describes Himself as our Advocate with the Father. These passages invite careful, personal reading. Notice who is speaking and what He asks us to trust. Doctrine and Covenants 19:15–20 · Doctrine and Covenants 45:3–5 · Doctrine and Covenants 18:10–13 Explore the picture and scripture A place in the day An open book and notebook sit before a thoughtful reader. Choose a passage and linger with it. 2 Nephi 32:3 Mercy reaches beyond the grave Joseph F. Smith's vision describes the Savior's work among the righteous dead and the organization of messengers to carry the gospel to those who had not received it. The vision expands our view of His redeeming work while honoring the need for repentance and the ordinances of His gospel. Doctrine and Covenants 138:11–19, 29–35, 57–59 · 1 Peter 3:18–20 · 1 Peter 4:6 Look unto Him Christ's invitation to look to Him belongs in ordinary days as well as moments of crisis. Read His words about His wounds, fear, and faith together. Return to the same passage when your circumstances change; there may be more to hear. Doctrine and Covenants 6:32–37 · Doctrine and Covenants 50:40–42 Pause and reflect Which of His invitations would you like to carry with you this week? Write it in your own notebook and return to the complete passage. Continue · Repentance ↓ All chapters ↑ 08 · Repentance Sin, repentance, and forgiveness Come honestly Repentance begins with turning toward God. We recognize wrong, feel sorrow for it, confess, seek forgiveness, and forsake the sin. Where possible, we repair the harm. Serious sins require help from the appropriate priesthood leader. The process is personal and sincere; a checklist cannot measure a changed heart. Explore the picture and scripture An honest prayer A man bows his head in the quiet of his home. There is room to speak honestly with God. Enos 1:2–8 Official guide: Repentance . Scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 58:42–43 . A heart can turn Alma remembered Jesus Christ and cried for mercy. His account moves from anguish to joy. We need not expect everyone's experience to follow the same emotional timetable to trust the same Redeemer. Alma 36:17–21 · Luke 15:11–24 · Enos 1:2–8 Explore the picture and scripture Coming home An elderly father holds his returning son. Read the parable Jesus told about repentance and welcome. Luke 15:11–24 Pause and reflect What is one honest step I can take today? Choose a private prayer, a needed conversation, or a safe act of repair. Do not use an apology to demand reconciliation or place someone in danger. Making amends calls for sensitivity and respect for the other person's wishes. Seek trusted guidance when direct contact could cause further harm. Read the Church's recovery guide on making amends . Explore the picture and scripture Taking a step to make things right Two neighbors exchange a tool at a workshop door. Consider the practical work of making amends. Mosiah 27:35 Official Church study guide Repentance Explore how faith in Jesus Christ leads to sincere change, confession, forgiveness, and a new direction. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Official Church study guide Step 9: Wherever possible, make direct restitution to all persons we have harmed. Read practical guidance for making amends with humility, care, and respect for those affected. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Continue · Grace ↓ All chapters ↑ 09 · Grace Grace and becoming new Grace is God's gift through Jesus Christ. We do not purchase it by accumulating good deeds. His grace also helps us grow as we exercise faith and follow Him. Obedience can become a grateful response to His love, and weakness can become a place where we learn to rely on Him. Explore the picture and scripture Room for hope A woman sits with open scriptures and a quiet expression of gratitude. Consider the change Christ can bring to a heart. Mosiah 5:2 Official reading: Dieter F. Uchtdorf, The Gift of Grace . Ephesians 2:8–10 · Ether 12:27 · Moroni 10:32–33 · Mosiah 5:2–7 Pause and reflect Where am I trying to carry everything alone? What might accepting help from Christ look like in that part of my life? Explore the picture and scripture Listen to Him Jesus speaks while those around Him listen. Bring a question to His teachings. Matthew 11:28–30 Conference message · Watch or read The Gift of Grace Dieter F. Uchtdorf teaches about the gift of grace and the change it can bring to our lives. records.excerpt: An illustrated study of Jesus Christ and His Atonement, from the Pearl of Great Price through all the scriptures. Explore His love, sacrifice, Resurrection, repentance, grace, and healing.

records.title: Because He lives, we can begin again
records.text: Jesus Christ is at the heart of this study. His suffering in Gethsemane and on the cross, His death, and His Resurrection open the way home to our Heavenly Father. We come to Him with sins to forsake, sorrows to share, questions to ask, and hope that may still be small. He invites us to come. Begin with John 3:16–17 and the official Atonement of Jesus Christ study guide . Follow the story from the beginning, or choose the part you need today. Open any picture for its scripture and study options. The artwork offers reverent, imaginative scenes; the linked scriptures provide the accounts we study.

records.title: Before the world: chosen from the beginning
records.text: 01 · Before the world Before the world: chosen from the beginning The Beloved Son and the Father's will The Pearl of Great Price takes the story of redemption back before mortal life. Moses records the Beloved Son's willingness to do the Father's will and give Him the glory. Abraham describes the council before the world and the choice of one who would be sent. Jesus Christ's mission belongs within the Father's loving purpose for His children. Moses 4:1–4 · Abraham 3:22–28 · Moses 1:39 Explore the picture and scripture The heavens above us Stars fill the sky above still water. Let the quiet of this imagined landscape lead you to the scriptures about Jesus Christ, the Creator. Creation belongs to the story Moses records God creating through His Only Begotten. John's Gospel identifies the Word who was with God and through whom all things were made. The Savior who came into mortality is also the Creator. His love for the world is personal. We are also responsible for our own sins. Our need for Him includes both the death we cannot prevent and the sins from which we cannot cleanse ourselves.
