records.title: Missionary Work
records.text: His work throughout the world Invite Others to Come Unto Christ Discover how love, service, and the restored gospel invite people to Christ. “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.” Mark 16:15 Meet with Missionaries Explore Ways to Serve Christ's commission A call to teach, baptize, and help people follow Him After His Resurrection, Jesus Christ sent His disciples to teach all nations, baptize in His name, and help people live what He taught. Latter-day Saint missionary work continues from that commission. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations.” Matthew 28:19 Read the Savior's commission Jesus teaches His Apostles as they walk together. Their calling begins with following Him. Select the image to learn more and choose the full-size view. Restoration and early missionaries From a Book of Mormon in hand to a worldwide witness Missionary work began before the Church was formally organized and gathered momentum during Joseph Smith's lifetime. 1829–1830 The message begins to travel Early believers shared the Book of Mormon and testified of the Restoration even before the Church's organization. June 1830 Samuel Smith is called Joseph Smith's brother Samuel became the first missionary called after the Church was organized, carrying copies of the Book of Mormon through communities near Palmyra, New York. 1830s–1840s Missions cross borders and oceans Missionaries traveled through the United States and Canada and then to England and the Pacific, often serving at great personal sacrifice. Today Local disciples build a global Church Missionaries serve among many cultures and languages while local members and leaders nurture faith in their own communities. Carrying the message Samuel Smith began with a few books, a willing heart, and faith that the message would find those prepared to receive it. Crossing oceans Early missionaries left familiar homes and carried their witness into new nations, languages, and communities. Study Early Missionaries Explore the Growth of the Work One Savior, one invitation, carried with love throughout the world. The missionary purpose Help people draw closer to the Savior Missionaries do more than deliver a message. They help people build faith in Jesus Christ, turn toward Him, prepare for baptism, receive the gift of the Holy Ghost, and continue along the covenant path. That work is personal. It happens through prayer, scripture study, sincere conversation, patient listening, invitations to act in faith, and continued friendship. Read the Missionary Purpose Faith expressed through action What Missionaries Do Every assignment is different, but the work remains centered on Jesus Christ and the needs of God's children. 01 Teach of Jesus Christ Missionaries study the scriptures, share the restored gospel, answer questions, and testify of the Savior. 02 Listen and Invite They seek to understand each person, then offer simple invitations that help faith become personal action. 03 Serve with Love Missionaries lift burdens through practical service, community work, disaster cleanup, and everyday kindness. 04 Strengthen Communities They work with local members and leaders, support new friends, and help build belonging that continues after a visit. A pattern for every disciple Love, Share, Invite Sharing the gospel is not limited to full-time missionaries. It can grow naturally from Christlike love, honest friendship, and respect for each person's agency. Love See the person first Pray for people, listen without an agenda, and serve because they are children of God, not because you expect a particular response. Share Speak naturally of goodness Share what gives you hope in Jesus Christ through ordinary conversation, personal experience, scripture, and quiet example. Invite Open a door without pressure Offer a simple invitation to learn, worship, serve, or meet missionaries, then honor the answer with warmth and friendship. Explore Love, Share, Invite Every nation, kindred, tongue, and people A Worldwide Work, Lived One Person at a Time Missionaries serve across languages, cultures, cities, villages, and local communities. The setting changes, but the pattern remains: love people, respect their agency, teach clearly, and point them toward Jesus Christ. Scriptures that shape the work Study the invitation to serve and gather Matthew 28:19–20 Teach all nations The risen Lord commissions His disciples to teach, baptize, and trust His continuing presence. Doctrine and Covenants 4:3 Desires to serve The Lord connects a willing desire with a call to participate in His work. Doctrine and Covenants 18:15–16 Joy in helping souls return Missionary service finds its deepest joy in helping even one person come unto Jesus Christ. Mosiah 18:8–9 Bear one another's burdens Disciples witness of God through compassion, comfort, and a willingness to mourn with others. Called to serve Different Assignments, the Same Savior Missionary calls and assignments are suited to the missionary and to the needs of God's children. Listening before teaching Missionary lessons begin with people, their questions, and a sincere desire to help them draw closer to Jesus Christ. Serving side by side Young adults and senior couples offer different gifts while sharing the same purpose of loving and lifting God's children. Young adults Teaching Missionaries Young elders and sisters serve away from home, learn to teach the gospel, and invite people to come closer to Jesus Christ. Learn about teaching missions Local service Service Missionaries Young service missionaries live at home and serve God and His children through assignments shaped around local needs and individual capacity. Explore service missions Experience offered Senior Missionaries Senior couples and individuals may teach, support Church operations, strengthen local leaders, serve charities, and use a lifetime of experience to bless others. Discover senior opportunities A simple first conversation What Happens When You Meet Missionaries? You can meet at home, online, at church, or in another comfortable public place. Missionaries will listen to your questions, pray with you, read scripture with you, and discuss the teachings of Jesus Christ. Missionary visits are free. Choose a time and place. Meet in the setting that feels comfortable to you. Bring your questions. The conversation should begin with what matters to you. Decide your next step. You choose whether and how the conversation continues. Request a Missionary Visit Know What to Expect Continue the journey Choose a path to learn or serve Follow a trusted source, deepen your study, or begin a real conversation. Study Preach My Gospel Learn the doctrine, skills, and Christlike purpose that guide missionary service. Explore Church History Continue into source-grounded stories of the Restoration and the Church's worldwide growth. Discover Global Stories Use the official Church History collection to learn how faith took root in many places. Meet Missionaries Ask questions and learn about Jesus Christ in a free conversation arranged around you. Independent website. focusChrist is not an official website of, sponsored by, or endorsed by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Missionary information and next steps link to current official Church resources. Official Missionary Resources Ask a Gospel Question Watch, read, and reflect Faith shared through words and service These messages join personal testimony with sincere care for another person. Church video What Do Missionaries Do? See how missionaries seek to follow Jesus Christ by teaching His gospel and serving people. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video Missionary Work: Sharing What Is in Your Heart Explore simple, respectful ways disciples can love, share, and invite. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Continue with sharing and service Study before a conversation, or continue afterward Meeting missionaries can bring both curiosity and uncertainty. You can prepare by reading a short passage and bringing your own questions. You may ask what a term means, request the source of a teaching, or say that you need more time. A respectful conversation makes room for your background and your choices. In Matthew 28:18-20 , the risen Jesus commissions His disciples to teach and baptize, and promises His presence. Read the commission with its focus on Him. It explains the Christian invitation to discipleship; it does not remove another person's freedom to consider, ask, or decline an invitation. Start with Jesus Christ Learn what Latter-day Saints mean by His Atonement and Resurrection. Bring a question about how those beliefs shape daily discipleship. Read a passage before discussing the book Explore its purpose and try a focused reading. Separate questions about its teachings from questions about its origin. Consider the invitation to pray Study prayer and discernment without assuming everyone receives an answer in the same way or at the same speed. After a conversation, return to the original passage and write down what was explained, what you understood differently, and what remains open. You do not need to resolve every question in one visit.

records.title: Latter-day Saint Pioneer Stories
records.text: Faith across the journey Pioneer Faith & History Explore pioneer faith and history through stories, sources, and questions. Ask About Pioneers Ask a sincere question about Latter-day Saint pioneers and their history. Type your question below or click a topic. AI-assisted answers are study aids and may contain errors. Unreviewed questions and limited recent context may be sent to external AI providers for research and verification. Please do not submit sensitive personal information. PIONEER TOPICS The gathering begins From Nauvoo to Winter Quarters The westward story began with families leaving homes they had built, crossing the Mississippi River, and enduring the difficult first season in temporary settlements along the Missouri River. Leaving Nauvoo, 1846 Families crossed the Mississippi and began an uncertain journey west. Winter Quarters, 1846 to 1847 Temporary homes became places of preparation, worship, grief, and endurance. THE JOURNEY The Exodus Begins - February 1846 The first wagons left Nauvoo, Illinois, on February 4, 1846, beginning the westward exodus. The National Park Service estimates that nearly 70,000 Latter-day Saint emigrants followed the trail to the Great Salt Lake Valley from 1847 through 1868. Winter Quarters - 1846-1847 After crossing Iowa, the Saints established Winter Quarters on the west bank of the Missouri River in present-day Omaha, Nebraska. Other settlements and outfitting camps were established across the river in Iowa. Entering the Valley - July 21-24, 1847 Members of the advance company entered the Salt Lake Valley before Brigham Young, who was ill and traveling behind them. Young's carriage entered the camp on July 24, 1847. Pioneer Day - July 24, 1847 The arrival is celebrated. Today, Pioneer Day is a Utah state holiday commemorating this historic journey. 1850s-1900s Temple Square Development Temple Square evolves from a muddy lot to a spiritual center. The Tabernacle and other buildings transform the heart of Salt Lake City. 1853-1893 Salt Lake Temple Construction Construction of the Salt Lake Temple began in 1853. The temple was dedicated in 1893, forty years after the cornerstone ceremony. Handcart Companies - 1856-1860 Over 3,000 pioneers pull handcarts across the plains. The Martin and Willie handcart companies face tragic rescues in 1856. 1869 Transcontinental Railroad The golden spike was driven at Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869. The completed transcontinental railroad reduced a journey of months to days and brought the organized overland pioneer era to a close. January 4, 1896 Utah Statehood Utah became the 45th state on January 4, 1896, after a long and contested path from territory to statehood. Life between landmarks The trail was lived one day at a time Beyond the dates and destinations, the journey was made through ordinary work, long stretches beside the Platte River, and difficult crossings that required the strength of the entire company. Daily Life on the Trail Repairs, meals, animals, and family responsibilities continued with every mile. Westward Beside the Platte Companies followed the broad river corridor across the plains in natural traveling groups. Crossing the Rivers People, animals, and wagons worked together against current, rock, and cold water. THE TRAIL These landmarks trace the route; the general route labels do not give an arrival date for every company. The Church History Pioneer Sketches exhibit documents William Clayton’s June 21, 1847 visit to Independence Rock and places the surviving drawings in the wider trail landscape. 1846 Nauvoo, Illinois The organized exodus began here in February 1846 after violence, legal conflict, and pressure against the Latter-day Saints in Illinois. Wagons crossed the Mississippi River into Iowa Territory. 1846 Garden Grove, Iowa The pioneers established Garden Grove as an Iowa way station, where they planted crops and built shelters to help companies that followed. Winter 1846 Missouri River Settlements Winter Quarters stood in present-day Omaha, Nebraska, with additional camps and settlements across the river in Iowa. This Missouri River area became the principal staging and outfitting region for westward companies. 1847 route Chimney Rock, Nebraska Famous natural landmark on the trail. This distinctive rock formation served as a beacon for weary travelers crossing the plains. Summer 1847 Fort Laramie, Wyoming This established trading post on the North Platte River was an important landmark and resupply point on several western emigrant trails. June 21, 1847 Independence Rock, Wyoming This prominent granite landmark became known for the names and dates carved or painted by travelers on the western emigrant trails. William Clayton reached it with the vanguard company on June 21, 1847. 1847 route Sweetwater River, Wyoming The trail followed and repeatedly crossed the Sweetwater River. Devil's Gate, a narrow gorge cut by the river, became one of the route's best-known landmarks. 1847 route South Pass, Wyoming Crossing the Continental Divide. This gentle pass through the Rocky Mountains opened the way to the Great Basin. July 1847 Fort Bridger, Wyoming Fort Bridger was a trading post and landmark on the final portion of the route toward the Great Salt Lake Valley. July 1847 Echo Canyon, Utah The trail passed through this narrow canyon during the final mountain approach toward the Salt Lake Valley. July 1847 Emigration Canyon, Utah Steep canyon descent into the valley. Pioneers guide their wagons through narrow passages before emerging into Salt Lake Valley. July 21-24, 1847 Salt Lake Valley, Utah Members of the advance company entered the valley before Brigham Young arrived on July 24. The company began planting crops and digging irrigation ditches soon after arrival. 1857 Mountain Meadows, Utah The 1857 Mountain Meadows Massacre occurred far south of the main 1846-1847 pioneer route. It is included here only as a separate and painful episode in territorial Utah history; follow the official Church History topic for a sourced account. Faith under strain Handcarts, hardship, and rescue Most handcart companies reached the valley safely. The late departure of the Willie and Martin companies in 1856 placed them in severe autumn storms, where relief parties carried food, clothing, blankets, and hope east from Utah. The Handcart Journey, 1856 Families carried only what their carts and their own strength could bear. Rescue Wagons Arrive Relief parties met the companies with supplies, teams, shelter, and human care. Willie & Martin Companies July 1856 The Companies Depart Late The Willie and Martin handcart companies depart from Iowa City later than planned. The delay sets off a chain of events that will test faith and endurance to the limit. August-October 1856 Hardships Begin The late departure left the companies on the plains as food diminished and severe autumn weather approached. Snowstorms in October intensified the crisis. October 1856 Stranded in Wyoming Severe October snowstorms caught both companies in present-day Wyoming. Cold, hunger, exhaustion, and illness caused many deaths while rescuers traveled east from Utah. October 1856 The Rescue After learning that the companies were still on the trail, Brigham Young called for rescuers, wagons, food, clothing, and teams. Relief parties traveled east from the Salt Lake Valley and assisted the emigrants. November 4-9, 1856 Martin's Cove The Martin Company camped in the area now called Martin's Cove from November 4 to 9. The cove offered some shelter, but the emigrants continued to suffer from cold, hunger, illness, and exhaustion. November 1856 Arrival in Salt Lake The Willie Company reached Salt Lake City on November 9, and the Martin Company arrived on November 30. Residents received the survivors and helped provide food, clothing, and shelter. November 1856 The Faith and Legacy The Willie and Martin experience is remembered for suffering, rescue, faith, and the consequences of delayed departure and inadequate provisions. Claims about miracles, motives, or individual experiences should be tied to identified contemporary records rather than generalized tradition. A destination becomes a home Arrival was the beginning of another work Entering the valley ended the overland journey, but it began years of planting, building, worship, and community life. The same faith that carried pioneers west shaped what they built after arriving. First View of the Valley, 1847 The mountain passage opened onto the place where the advance company would begin planting. Building a New Community Irrigation, shelter, food, and shared labor turned arrival into settlement. Building the Salt Lake Temple, 1853 to 1893 Four decades of work made the temple a lasting expression of covenant and sacrifice. The Ask experience above also uses Tell My Story, Too to identify a pioneer before corroborating the selected person through authoritative records. September 12, 1856 Franklin D. Richards “They were considerably weakened ... but were in good spirits.” Diary passage describing the Willie handcart company near North Bluff Creek. Read the transcript Spring 1856 James G. Jones “There were two of us and hundreds needing help.” Jones's account of encountering the handcart company during the rescue. Oaks Sharing the Gospel Consider the qualities of a Christlike invitation. Faith During Trials Trusting Jesus Christ through grief, uncertainty, adversity, and difficult decisions. These destinations provide broader video and study collections when you want to explore beyond a single message. Jesus Christ Videos Life, mission, teachings, Resurrection, and relevance of Jesus Christ. Bible Videos Scripture stories centered on the Savior, His Apostles, miracles, and teachings. Gospel Video & Images Church-created media for scripture, Book of Mormon, Jesus Christ, and gospel study. General Conference Current and past messages organized by conference, speaker, and topic. Not sure where to continue? Start with the question you have now Use Ask for a sincere question about Jesus Christ, scripture, Latter-day Saint belief, or Church history. The permanent Answer Library and Art & Study paths are also available for browsing. Church video Look Unto Christ: January 2025 Discussion Listen for ways to turn attention toward the Savior. Choose one invitation to consider alongside D&C 6:36. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video Look Unto Christ: Worldwide Event for Youth A message with President Jeffrey R. Holland and youth leaders. Consider how trust in Christ can shape your next faithful step. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Read the signature scripture study Turn a short message into a thoughtful study A short video can introduce a subject without giving it all the context it deserves. After watching, write down its main claim or question. Open the named scripture and read the surrounding verses: who is speaking, what is happening, and what problem is being addressed? Notice which parts of the message come directly from the text and which are the speaker's interpretation or application. For a resurrection message, for example, John 20:1-31 supplies a sequence of witnesses and the author's purpose, not simply a hopeful phrase. The Living Christ study walks through that sequence. From there, the life-after-death study explores the next question about resurrection and human hope. If a message raises a concern rather than offering comfort, keep that question. You can reread the source, explore another study, or pause. A meaningful response does not have to be immediate or positive. The theme links above are places to continue learning, not a requirement to consume more content.

records.title: Turn a short message into a thoughtful study
records.pageTitle: Watch & Study Jesus Christ: Videos, Scripture & Hope
records.text: A short video can introduce a subject without giving it all the context it deserves. After watching, write down its main claim or question. Open the named scripture and read the surrounding verses: who is speaking, what is happening, and what problem is being addressed? Notice which parts of the message come directly from the text and which are the speaker's interpretation or application. For a resurrection message, for example, John 20:1-31 supplies a sequence of witnesses and the author's purpose, not simply a hopeful phrase. The Living Christ study walks through that sequence. From there, the life-after-death study explores the next question about resurrection and human hope. If a message raises a concern rather than offering comfort, keep that question. You can reread the source, explore another study, or pause. A meaningful response does not have to be immediate or positive. The theme links above are places to continue learning, not a requirement to consume more content.
